## DAILY BRIEFING

### 1. CIA director held sensitive talks in Moscow
CIA Director John Ratcliffe met Russian intelligence officials during an unannounced Moscow visit. Ukraine and Poland said Washington had briefed them, while reports indicated discussions covered Ukraine, Russian support for Iran, and the possibility of Russian action against a NATO member. President Donald Trump denied that Ratcliffe carried a specific warning.

**Why it matters:** The visit represents a rare high-level intelligence channel between Washington and Moscow amid stalled peace efforts and concern about broader Russian escalation. Its precise purpose remains unclear.

### 2. Ukraine plans a major expansion of long-range drone attacks
President Volodymyr Zelensky ordered Ukraine to work toward launching 1,000 long-range drones daily, up from more than 300 strikes on average. Ukraine also reported attacks on the Yaroslavl oil refinery and a Tu-95 strategic bomber at Engels airbase, and claimed drone operations had effectively confined Russian warships to Novorossiysk.

**Why it matters:** Kyiv is increasingly targeting Russia’s energy, naval and strategic aviation infrastructure to raise the economic and military costs of continuing the war.

### 3. Russian strikes are putting growing pressure on Ukrainian logistics
Ukrainian officials said Russian attacks have destroyed about 90 percent of the country’s modern commercial storage capacity. A new strike set warehouses ablaze near Kyiv and temporarily closed part of the main Kyiv–Chop highway.

**Why it matters:** Although officials said there is no immediate famine risk, sustained attacks on warehouses and distribution networks could increase costs, reduce product availability and weaken Ukraine’s civilian resilience.

### 4. Ukraine signals a prolonged war and acute manpower requirements
Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people monthly and warned that a near-term end to the war is unrealistic. The government is also seeking easier residency and citizenship pathways for foreign military volunteers.

**Why it matters:** The statements underscore Ukraine’s continuing personnel shortages, domestic tensions surrounding mobilization and preparations for an extended conflict.

### 5. Gaza ceasefire faces renewed risk of collapse
Board of Peace envoy Nikolay Mladenov warned that failures by both Israel and the Palestinian side to follow the agreed roadmap could cause the ceasefire to collapse. He said preparations had been made for an International Stabilization Force, with Morocco agreeing to participate, although Israel has publicly disputed key elements of the plan.

**Why it matters:** The roadmap’s contested status and continuing Israeli attacks leave both the ceasefire and proposed postwar governance arrangements vulnerable.

## WATCH

- **Russia–NATO escalation signals:** Reports that Moscow may view NATO-supplied weapons and intelligence as direct alliance involvement, and may intensify attacks on Ukraine, remain unconfirmed but warrant close attention.
- **Scale and effects of Ukraine’s drone campaign:** Monitor whether Kyiv can approach its 1,000-drone target and whether strikes materially disrupt Russian fuel supplies, ports or strategic aviation.
- **Gaza stabilization force:** Watch for the announced arrival of advance elements and whether Israel accepts their deployment and mandate.

### Taiwan Raises Warning Over Chinese Election Interference

**What happened:** Taiwan’s governing Democratic Progressive Party identified seven forms of suspected Chinese election interference ahead of year-end local elections, including subsidized voter tours, foreign-funded propaganda, fabricated polling and intermediary funding networks. It said violations could carry prison terms of up to 15 years, while eligible informants could receive rewards of up to NT$20 million.

**Why it matters:** The warning highlights continuing concern over political influence operations targeting Taiwan. Enforcement actions or accusations during the campaign could intensify domestic political tensions and further strain cross-Strait relations.

### SK Hynix Expands US-Based AI Chip Supply Chain

**What happened:** South Korean chipmaker SK Hynix began construction of a more than US$4 billion high-bandwidth memory packaging facility in Indiana. The US-supported plant is expected to begin mass production in 2029, packaging and testing wafers manufactured in South Korea.

**Why it matters:** High-bandwidth memory is critical to advanced AI systems. The investment strengthens US-South Korean technology integration, addresses a US weakness in advanced semiconductor packaging and shifts part of a strategically important Asian supply chain onto US territory.

### Taiwan Warns of Severe Long-Term Population Decline

**What happened:** Taiwan’s National Development Council projected that the population would fall nearly 48 percent to 12.15 million by 2075. People aged 65 or older are forecast to constitute 52.9 percent of the population by then, while the working-age share falls to 42.3 percent.

**Why it matters:** A smaller and older workforce could constrain Taiwan’s manufacturing, semiconductor and AI industries while increasing pressure on public finances and social services. The outlook raises the importance of automation, higher labor participation and overseas talent recruitment.

### WATCH

- **Taiwan energy policy:** A nuclear-power referendum will be held alongside local elections, as Taiwan prepares major gas-fired expansion while facing uncertain electricity demand from AI data centers.
- **Russia’s Asian engagement:** Senior representatives from China, Indonesia, Mongolia and Myanmar are scheduled to join President Vladimir Putin at the Eastern Economic Forum, offering a measure of Moscow’s continuing regional partnerships.

## 1. US and Russia Hold High-Level Intelligence Talks

CIA Director John Ratcliffe made an unannounced visit to Moscow and met Russian intelligence officials. The Kremlin confirmed the talks and said President Vladimir Putin was briefed, although he did not meet Ratcliffe. Reports differ on the mission’s purpose, citing possible efforts to revive Ukraine negotiations, warn against escalation involving NATO, or convey assessments of Russia’s military and economic position. Ukraine said Washington briefed Kyiv before and after the meetings.

**Why it matters:** The visit establishes a direct, senior-level channel amid stalled peace efforts and concern that Russia could intensify operations against Ukraine or Western interests. The conflicting accounts also indicate uncertainty over whether the talks produced any concrete reduction in escalation risks.

## 2. Ukraine Plans Major Expansion of Long-Range Drone Strikes

President Volodymyr Zelensky ordered Ukraine to work toward launching 1,000 long-range drones per day against Russia, up from what he described as more than 300 strikes daily. Ukraine also reported attacks on the Yaroslavl oil refinery and a Tu-95 strategic bomber at Engels air base, while Zelensky claimed drone operations had restricted shipping at Novorossiysk.

**Why it matters:** A sustained expansion would increase pressure on Russian energy revenue, military aviation and Black Sea logistics. It would also deepen the war’s reach inside Russia and could prompt stronger Russian retaliation or additional measures to protect strategic infrastructure.

## 3. Ukraine Signals Prolonged War and Acute Manpower Needs

Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov said Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people each month and warned that ending the war soon is unrealistic. His comments came amid public dissatisfaction with mobilization and discussion of major changes to the draft system. Kyiv is also considering easier residency rules for foreign veterans as it seeks additional personnel.

**Why it matters:** Ukraine’s ability to replace casualties and sustain frontline units remains central to its war effort. Mobilization reforms could affect military readiness, domestic stability and public confidence, particularly after years of fighting without a clear path to demobilization for many troops.

## WATCH

- **Russian escalation:** Monitor reports that Moscow is considering heavier ballistic-missile attacks on Kyiv and whether intelligence contacts with Washington reduce that risk.
- **Economic and logistics pressure:** Russian attacks have reportedly destroyed much of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity, while Ukrainian strikes increasingly target Russian refineries and ports. Further disruption could materially affect both countries’ wartime economies.

## Iran conflict shifts toward economic pressure and Hormuz diplomacy

Six months into the conflict, large-scale US-Israeli air operations have slowed, but Washington is maintaining substantial forces in the region and intensifying economic pressure. The US moved to restrict the UAE branches of Egypt’s Banque Misr from the US financial system over alleged support for Iran. Tehran said it remains open to diplomacy and has agreed with Oman on a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, but linked reopening the waterway to US compliance with an earlier memorandum, including sanctions and blockade relief.

**Why it matters:** Continued closure or disruption of Hormuz threatens a critical global energy route. The combination of a US naval counterblockade, sanctions and unresolved Iranian conditions leaves significant risks of economic disruption and renewed military escalation.

## Gaza ceasefire roadmap at risk

Board of Peace representative Nikolay Mladenov warned that failures by Israel and the Palestinian side to follow the proposed roadmap could collapse the Gaza ceasefire. The plan covers reconstruction, the disarmament of Palestinian armed groups, gradual Israeli withdrawal, a technocratic Palestinian administration and deployment of an International Stabilization Force. Morocco has reportedly agreed to participate, while Israel vetoed Turkish involvement. Israel’s government has publicly disputed or rejected key aspects of the plan.

**Why it matters:** The conflicting positions threaten a return to major hostilities and could delay humanitarian relief and reconstruction. The dispute also complicates efforts by Qatar, Egypt and Türkiye to sustain negotiations and establish postwar governance arrangements.

## Rare Israeli air strike in Jenin signals West Bank escalation

An Israeli air strike near Jenin killed three Palestinians. Israel described one target as a Hamas operative, while Palestinian Islamic Jihad said all three were members of its armed wing and identified Qais Bitawi as a senior commander. The strike was a rare use of air power in the occupied West Bank. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz also said Israeli forces were now permanently stationed in the Jenin refugee camp.

**Why it matters:** The operation suggests a more aggressive and potentially sustained Israeli military posture in the northern West Bank. It could intensify armed confrontation, displacement and tensions between Israel, Palestinian factions and the Palestinian Authority.

## WATCH

- **Gaza stabilization force:** Whether advance elements deploy despite Israel’s stated objections, and whether the proposed Palestinian technocratic committee assumes administrative responsibilities.
- **Mecca defence pact:** Reports suggest Iran’s possible involvement has been discussed, but Tehran says it has received no formal invitation. Any formal talks could reshape emerging regional security arrangements involving Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan.

### U.S. expands reliance on commercial space intelligence

**What happened:** A Government Accountability Office report found that the U.S. Space Force spent nearly $124 million on commercial space data and analytical services from January 2023 through September 2025. The National Reconnaissance Office separately averaged $300–500 million in annual spending, while the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency averaged $25–125 million. The Space Force says its fiscal 2027 request includes more than $2.5 billion for a broader range of commercial capabilities and services.

**Why it matters:** Greater use of private-sector imagery, sensing and interference-detection services could improve the resilience and speed of U.S. military space operations. It also increases the operational importance of commercial providers and highlights unresolved procurement and regulatory barriers.

### Pentagon considers another senior-leadership summit

**What happened:** Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is reportedly considering summoning hundreds of generals and admirals to Marine Corps Base Quantico for a second senior-leadership address. No date or attendance requirements have been confirmed. A previous meeting was used to announce directives emphasizing warfighting, readiness, physical standards and the reversal of diversity initiatives.

**Why it matters:** Another gathering could signal additional department-wide changes affecting military standards, force management and strategic priorities. Its scale and short-notice format would also make any resulting directives consequential across the U.S. armed forces.

### Mexico’s disappearances crisis has wider impact on children

**What happened:** Tejiendo Redes Infancia estimated that approximately 165,000 Mexican children and adolescents could have a missing parent. The estimate is based on 103,176 missing people aged 15–49 and the national average number of children per person. Mexico’s missing-person registry does not systematically record affected children or the support they receive.

**Why it matters:** The findings underscore the broader human-security consequences of Mexico’s disappearance crisis, including lost household income, disrupted education and increased vulnerability. Data gaps may prevent authorities from recognizing these children as indirect victims and allocating targeted assistance.

### WATCH

- **U.S. defense directives:** Whether the proposed Quantico meeting occurs and produces new force-wide policies.
- **Commercial space procurement:** Congressional action on fiscal 2027 funding and efforts to convert commercial demonstrations into operational military programs.

articles.title: Both Trump and Putin feel backed into a corner
articles.body:
analysis
CIA chief's confusing Moscow trip reminds us of the corners Trump and Putin are in
Remember the Central Intelligence Agency? The US intelligence agency which once seemed to wander the world creating wars and instability and inspiring countless thrillers?
You don't seem to hear so much about the CIA these days. Who needs a bunch of shadowy spooks to create world chaos when you have the US president doing it all by himself?
But the CIA has been back in the headlines this week after it was revealed its director, John Ratcliffe, had just made a trip to Moscow, variously described in US media as "mysterious" or "a surprise", to talk to his Russian counterparts.
Intriguingly (as all spooky things invariably should be) that is about all the media reports agree upon.
Different theories on mysterious trip
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow on Wednesday that Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during his time in the Russian capital, but that he didn't meet with Putin. Putin was briefed on the talks, Peskov said.
Depending on whether you read the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal or the Washington Post, Ratcliffe may have met with the head of Russia's FSB intelligence service, or the foreign intelligence service, the SVR, or both.
But what is most striking about the reporting of this meeting is the different spin on the apparent reason for the unexpected trip.
The New York Times reported that Ratcliffe went to Moscow "to privately share his bleak assessment of the state of the Russian war against Ukraine, and to urge the Russians to cut a deal before their military and economic situation gets worse".
The Washington Post reported Ratcliffe's trip was "preceded by fresh US intelligence indicating that the Kremlin sees the United States as weakened by the Iran war, offering Russia an opportunity to escalate action against American interests and allies in Europe".
The Wall Street Journal hedged its bets by saying the mission was "so sensitive that even some senior White House officials didn't know about it ahead of time".
Trump, the Journal said, had "personally dispatched" Ratcliffe "after previous rounds of negotiations using other trusted envoys failed to stop the fighting in Russia's war with Ukraine".
"Over the past few months, Moscow has escalated its attacks on Ukraine, boosted support for Iran's regime and resisted American attempts to improve economic ties," it noted.
Putin escalates threats against Europe
The US president has unleashed quite a lot of self-inflicted damage on his country — let alone his political fortunes — in the past week: think a secondary sanctions regime against Iranian trading partners and a trade war with Canada which will hurt US industry and hurt the Republicans in the mid-terms.
Yet these contradictory narratives on the CIA chief's travels to Moscow seem to best highlight the impotent flailing on almost all global issues of the Trump administration, an administration which some analysts still endeavour to argue has a strategy, in the face of repeated signs that it has none. On anything.
Remember when Trump came back to the White House claiming to have a good relationship with Putin and that he could end the war in Ukraine within 24 hours?
Putin, in the same period since Trump's return, has looked like he was winning, and more recently like he was losing.
What Putin does seem to have been doing most recently is escalating his threats against other European countries — a development which potentially makes all of those newspapers' assessments true at the same time.
There's been more covert hybrid warfare, airspace incursions and direct military threats, notably this week against the UK and France.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham had promised Ukraine it would allow the besieged nation access to classified technology to start its own production of Storm Shadow long-range cruise missiles. France has also agreed to supply missile technology.
Russia's foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova said on Thursday the two countries were "playing with fire", and of "inevitable catastrophic consequences" for British military installations both within Ukraine and elsewhere.
Trump in a corner on Iran
So now we have two autocrats — Trump and Putin — both stepping up their aggressive language and apparently feeling cornered at the same time.
Both of them are in very tight spots.
Trump has nowhere to go in his conflict with Iran. In fact, he's not able to claim any great victories in any of his foreign policy initiatives.
World leaders seem to be increasingly just ignoring him, or standing up to him — like Canada's Mark Carney this week over tariffs.
Even the "break glass" option of distractions didn't work: possible talks mooted for later this year with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un got no immediate love from Pyongyang.
That was despite Trump citing his strong personal relationship with the North Korean leader, and the fact it followed Trump's directive to the Pentagon to shorten military exercises with South Korea.
Putin's Russia, meanwhile, has also threatened to attack European defence companies and factories, and has escalated a "shadow war" in Europe.
Intelligence agencies have laid the blame at Russia's door for an attack on a Ukranian military cargo aircraft at an airport in Germany; mysterious fires on drone and munitions factories in Estonia, Italy and Bulgaria; and talk of assassination attempts on drone manufacturers.
That's in addition to a major rise in airspace violations by Russian drones and fighter aircraft, particularly over Poland, Finland and Romania, and an explosive-laden Russian maritime drone floating close to Europe's largest offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
NATO released a statement after its August 12 meeting condemning repeated Russian airspace violations which it said were not only "dangerous and unacceptable" but also observing that they demonstrated "Russia's increasing tolerance for risk".
Loading
'Two to three' week conflict hits six months
While Trump rails against Canada with colourful but pointless moves like unilaterally declaring Lake Ontario will be renamed Lake America, Putin would not need any great secret intelligence sources to assess that, whatever the state of the ground war in Ukraine, the US does seem at a low point in its capacity to do anything about changing the dynamics of that conflict.
Trump could well have got the CIA chief to tell Russian intelligence counterparts, as the Wall Street Journal reported, that the US remained committed to NATO's Article 5, which says that an attack on one member is considered an attack on all.
But like the rest of the world, the Russian leader would know of the depletion of US military hardware, the damage done to its US bases in the Middle East, and its troop shortfalls, as illustrated by its problems in its aircraft carrier fleet, which have also alarmed allies in our region.
Trump dismissed questions about the Ratcliffe trip on Thursday, saying "he's not going to be attacking a NATO territory".
But the concern that one leader under pressure may escalate pressure on another leader under pressure by opening new fronts in Europe, or increase the pressure by maintaining or even increasing its ties with Iran, are real.
The Trump administration seems equally powerless to control the economic fallout of its own policies on the US economy or for that matter the world economy.
US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent has perplexed financial markets this week with ineffective interventions in the US Treasury bond market designed to bring down long term US interest rates, even as the US Federal Reserve is under pressure to increase rates because of the inflationary impacts of Trump's war in the Middle East and burgeoning debt at home.
This week marked six months of a conflict with Iran which was allegedly only going to take two to three weeks at most.
The fallout from that decision sees Trump, his administration, and global geopolitics instead bogged down in a multitude of strategic and economic quagmires.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people monthly, Budanov says
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people monthly, Budanov says
Key developments on Aug. 28:
- Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people per month, Budanov says, warning war won't end soon
- Ukrainian drones target one of Russia's largest oil refineries in Yaroslavl, Tu-95 bomber at Engels base in overnight attack
- Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern storage facilities, minister says
- Russia considers placing troops, weapons on civilian ships as it struggles to protect shadow fleet, Zelensky says
- Russian attack destroys one of Ukraine's largest vodka plants
Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov has warned that Ukraine cannot afford to mobilize less than 30,000 people per month, as ending the war in the short term is "unrealistic."
The comments, made on Aug. 28 on Ukrainian television, come as Ukraine's leadership is under increasing pressure from both the military and society to tackle issues in the country's flawed and unpopular mobilization process.
Forced mobilization, as a part of martial law, has been in place in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
Since the draft ramped up in scope over last years as less Ukrainians volunteered to fight, mobilization has been a source of simmering tension in Ukrainian society. Cases of attacks on draft officers increased in frequency over 2026.
Ukraine requires a consistent flow of new recruits to stay in the fight, with Moscow showing no signs of stopping its war and increasing signs that a new mobilization wave in Russia could follow State Duma elections in autumn.
"No matter how much we say that we will call differently now, the quantitative indicators will not change, which means that the number of dissatisfied people will not change either," said Budanov.
In the interview, Budanov also urged Ukrainians not to believe that an end to the war could be around the corner.
"I think very soon everyone will see negotiations, but it will be more about the technical side and preparation for something big, which I hope we will get to someday," he said.
"We will not stop the war now. Not because we don't want to, it's just not realistic."
read also
Ukrainian drones target one of Russia's largest oil refineries in Yaroslavl, Tu-95 bomber at Engels base in overnight attack
Ukrainian drones struck the Yaroslavl oil refinery, one of Russia's largest oil processing facilities, overnight on Aug. 28, the General Staff confirmed, with attacks also reported on Moscow and the region.
In a separate operation a Tu-95 strategic heavy bomber was damaged at Engels air base in Saratov Oblast, President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
The target of the attack was the Slavneft-YANOS refinery, one of Russia's largest oil processing facilities, the General Staff said, adding that damage to the refinery was still being assessed.
The Slavneft-YANOS refinery, located about 250 kilometers (150 miles) northeast of Moscow and roughly 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Ukraine's border, processes around 15 million tons of oil per year, making it one of Russia's five largest oil refineries.
Ukrainian forces also targeted a Tu-95 in a separate operation. The strategic bomber is one of Russia's main platforms for mass cruise missile attacks against Ukraine and often operates from Engels Air Base, more than 600 kilometers (370 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
According to Zelensky, the successful strike on the plane was carried out by the Alpha special forces unit of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), the same unit that carried out Operation Spiderweb in June 2025, using small truck-launched drones to strike strategic bombers at airfields deep inside Russian territory.
read also
Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern storage facilities, minister says
Russian strikes have destroyed 90% of Ukraine's modern storage facilities for various types of goods, Agricultural Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on Aug. 28 during a press briefing at Interfax-Ukraine.
The statement comes as Russia has intensified attacks aimed at disrupting Ukrainian businesses by striking warehouses and logistics centers where goods are stored.
Vysotskyi said attacks on logistics infrastructure could affect the range of goods available in stores, but assured that there is no risk of Ukrainians running out of food.
"There is no threat of hunger," Vysotskyi added.
The continued destruction of warehouses is forcing businesses to find alternative ways to move and store goods. The most realistic option under the current circumstances is for suppliers to deliver goods directly to production or retail sites, bypassing long-term warehouse storage, according to the minister.
The minister added that some businesses are relocating to other areas, but Russian attacks have already reached some of these relocated facilities.
The minister also advocated for an equal distribution of risks among supply-chain participants when goods are destroyed by Russian attacks, emphasizing that the state is not involved in their commercial or contractual relations.
read also
Russia considers placing troops, weapons on civilian ships as it struggles to protect shadow fleet, Zelensky says
Russia is considering arming civilian vessels with small arms and electronic warfare equipment and deploying military personnel aboard them amid difficulties protecting its shadow fleet, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 28, citing a report by military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko.
Russia relies on a vast shadow fleet of aging tankers operating under opaque ownership structures and flags of convenience to export oil and petroleum products despite Western sanctions.
The Kremlin is considering these measures because the Russian navy can no longer safely escort Russian vessels to its Black Sea ports, according to Zelensky.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) assessed that Ukrainian drone strikes have effectively confined Russian warships to the port of Novorossiysk on the southeastern Black Sea, Zelensky added.
Some segments of Russia's exports have declined by as much as 80% in August, according to Zelensky.
The president also praised recent Ukrainian deep strikes, saying attacks on the Kombinat Kamenskiy plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast had "significantly limited" Russia's capacity to produce solid-fuel rocket motors, while operations at the Kstovo oil refinery in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod Oblast had also been halted.
At the same time, Zelensky said Russia plans to increase missile production, citing updated intelligence.
"All supplies of components, equipment, and machine tools that Russia uses to manufacture missiles must be completely blocked," Zelensky said.
read also
Russian attack destroys one of Ukraine's largest vodka plants
One of Ukraine’s largest vodka plants was destroyed beyond repair after Russia attacked Zaporizhzhia Oblast on Aug. 27.
The Khortytsia Distillery, launched in 2003 by Global Spirits, a Ukrainian firm headquartered in the U.S., was hit four times, sparking a three-hour-long fire, the company’s press service told Ukrainian media outlet NV.
Some of the products were completely destroyed by the fire, while others partially melted, the company said. In total, around 3 million to 4 million bottles of spirits were lost, on which the company had already paid excise taxes.
It’s not the first time Global Spirits has been targeted by a Russian attack, as Moscow stepped up strikes on Ukrainian businesses over the summer. On July 19, the company’s main warehouse was severely damaged in an attack, costing Global Spirits Hr 100 million ($2.2 million) in lost products.
The economic war has intensified in recent months, with Ukraine striking Russian oil facilities and e-commerce centers, and Moscow launching a mass campaign against retailers, shopping malls, supermarkets, ports, steel producers, gas stations, and postal services.

articles.title: Zelensky Says US Briefed Ukraine on CIA-Moscow Meetings
articles.body:
Ukraine received information from the US regarding several meetings CIA Director John Ratcliffe held with Russian intelligence officials, following his unannounced trip to Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Friday, Aug. 28, that Kyiv had discussed the developments with US officials before and after the Moscow meetings. He also thanked the American side for sharing information and for what he called the necessary tone in its diplomatic contacts with Russia.

articles.title: Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
articles.body:
Iran may be the key to the Mecca Pact’s future
The reported invitation for Iran to join the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement puts a new perspective on what the new alliance might ultimately become.
Mehdi Rahimi, head of the Iranian parliament’s news agency, said that the proposal was under consideration by the country’s leadership and argued that the creation of a regional security umbrella would represent a victory for the Islamic Republic. Shortly afterwards, however, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei stated that Tehran had received no formal invitation, although proposals for dialogue with the pact’s members on collective regional security had indeed been raised. For the moment, this appears to be a political overture intended to test the reactions of the parties rather than the beginning of a formal accession process. Even so, it suggests that the agreement is not intended as an alliance against Tehran, but as the possible foundation of a security system built with Iranian participation.
The Mecca Agreement was signed on August 7 by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif. Its central provision declares that an armed attack against one member will be regarded as an attack against all. The formula theoretically combines a formidable set of capabilities: Saudi Arabia’s immense financial resources and influence over global energy markets, Türkiye’s large military and sophisticated defence industry, and Pakistan’s substantial military experience and nuclear arsenal. Yet the public statements offer no detailed decision-making procedure and do not specify what action each signatory would be obliged to take during a crisis. At this stage, the pact is only a political declaration of collective deterrence and not a proper military alliance.
Erosion of the American monopoly
Donald Trump welcomed the pact and expressed satisfaction that the states of the region were finally assuming greater responsibility for their own defense. His response was consistent with his longstanding view that Washington’s allies should bear a larger share of military expenditure, allowing the US to reduce its costs and step back from the role of unconditional guarantor of other nations’ security. Seen from this perspective, the agreement might appear to be a success for American policy, since three US partners are establishing an additional mechanism of deterrence without Washington’s direct involvement.
Yet behind this public enthusiasm lies a trend that is far less favorable to the US. The Mecca Pact cannot be described as the first symptom of declining American influence in the Middle East, but it is the clearest institutional sign to date that regional powers no longer regard the American security umbrella as sufficient and have begun constructing autonomous centers of power. Washington retains its military bases, weapons systems, intelligence capabilities and relationships with regional elites, but it is gradually losing its monopoly over the rules by which Middle Eastern security is organized.
The US-Israeli war against Iran accelerated this transformation because it revealed the double-edged nature of American security guarantees. The US military presence may deter adversaries, but it can also draw the Gulf states into conflicts whose timing and objectives are determined without their meaningful participation. Iranian strikes, disruption to maritime trade and threats to energy infrastructure demonstrated that a close partnership with Washington does not insulate regional states from danger and may instead force them to bear the consequences of American policy.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan are not abandoning American weapons or political ties, yet they want a mechanism capable of functioning even when Washington’s priorities diverge from their own.
Iran could transform the pact into a security system
For the pact’s three founding members, the possibility of inviting Iran addresses a problem that might otherwise have become the source of another major conflict. As long as Tehran remained outside the agreement, it could interpret the partnership between Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan as an attempt to build a Sunni military bloc directed against the Islamic Republic.
By offering Tehran a place at the table, the pact’s founders have effectively replaced the question of whom the alliance is directed against with the question of which rules the region’s principal powers are prepared to accept. Even if Iran never joins, the dialogue itself reduces the likelihood that the agreement will automatically become an instrument of its isolation. Saudi Arabia gains an opportunity to combine military deterrence with continued diplomatic de-escalation, Türkiye strengthens its role as a mediator, and Pakistan avoids having to choose between its strategic partnership with Riyadh and its relationship with neighboring Iran.
Full Iranian participation could transform the nature of the pact itself. It would cease to be an alliance among states united by similar fears and would instead become a mechanism of mutual restraint in which one member’s security could not be achieved through another’s vulnerability. A declaration of collective defense alone, however, would not be enough. The participants would need emergency communication channels, rules for preventing military incidents, mechanisms for exchanging information on missile launches, guarantees of freedom of navigation and commitments not to support armed action against fellow members.
The most difficult issue would concern the non-state armed groups aligned with Iran. If Tehran joined the pact, it would inevitably be expected to assume political responsibility for the actions of forces receiving Iranian weapons and support. At the same time, the other members would have to refrain from exploiting Iran’s internal divisions as a means of exerting pressure on its leadership. Only such reciprocity could turn an appealing formula into a functioning regional order.
The economic prospects
Iran’s potential inclusion could initiate not only a political renaissance but also a major economic advance, since the development of the Middle East has been constrained for decades not by a lack of resources, but by chronic uncertainty. Wars raise shipping insurance costs, compel governments to accumulate weapons, discourage long-term investment and turn transport corridors into instruments of geopolitical bargaining. Even a partial reduction in these risks would release resources currently devoted to preparing for the next crisis.
Saudi capital, Turkish industry, the Pakistani market and Iran’s energy and transit potential could complement one another. Their cooperation could create new routes connecting Central Asia, the Persian Gulf, the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, while the security of the Strait of Hormuz could be transformed from an instrument of mutual coercion into a shared interest. A region long seen as mostly a theater of war and foreign intervention would gain an opportunity to become an autonomous economic center within an increasingly multipolar world.
The economic dividend, however, is not guaranteed. Continuing sanctions against Iran, competition over transport routes, clashing Turkish and Saudi ambitions, and Pakistan’s disputes with India could import old conflicts into the new arrangement. The pact’s success will depend on the ability of its members to separate collective security from temporary alignments and to prevent every bilateral confrontation from becoming an obligation for the entire coalition.
Israel’s choice
The most difficult external question concerns the future relationship between the Mecca Pact and Israel. Israel is already uneasy about the agreement, and would likely find the accession of Iran unacceptable, seeing it as the beginning of strategic encirclement.
Even with Iran, however, the pact does not have to become an alliance against Israel. If its members firmly establish the defensive nature of the agreement and offer Israel mechanisms for preventing conflict, it could restrain escalation rather than prepare the ground for it. The problem is that the current Israeli leadership has grown accustomed to pursuing security through the unrestricted use of unilateral force, whereas a regional system requires agreed rules and recognition that neighboring states also possess legitimate security interests.
Much will become clearer after the Knesset election scheduled for October 27, 2026. If Benjamin Netanyahu and the far-right bloc remain in power, tensions are likely to intensify, particularly if Israel continues its strikes against Iran and Syria while treating Türkiye’s growing influence as a direct threat. In that event, the Mecca Pact may evolve not simply as an alternative to weakening American guarantees, but as an instrument for deterring Israeli military action.
An opposition victory would not guarantee peace, since a hard line on Iran and national security extends far beyond Netanyahu’s political camp. Nevertheless, a new coalition might choose normalization over the endless expansion of conflict and attempt to incorporate Israel into the emerging regional balance.
The Mecca Agreement is not a new Middle East Order – merely a promise of one. Yet if it manages to accommodate Iran as a member, establish clear rules of mutual restraint and find a form of peaceful coexistence with Israel, the Middle East could for the first time in decades have a security system created primarily by the states of the region. Such a system would not eliminate their differences, but it could allow them to work with and around those differences without constant recourse to an external hegemon and without turning every crisis into a war. The cradle of the Abrahamic faiths might then cease to be consumed by recurring fires and begin its transformation into a strong, interconnected and prosperous region.

articles.title: Ukraine dismissed its defense minister in July. He is now advising NATO country on defense innovation
articles.body:
A NATO country's defense minister wanted Mykhailo Fedorov the day after Ukraine dismissed him. Fedorov, Ukraine's former defense minister, has agreed to advise Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto on defense innovation, he wrote on Telegram.
As deputy prime minister and digital transformation minister, Fedorov created the Brave1 defense-tech cluster, then ran the Defense Ministry from 14 January 2026 until his dismissal in July. The removal triggered nationwide protests through July, with demonstrators calling for his reinstatement.
Earlier, Fedorov refused every other post Zelenskyy offered, saying only the defense minister, the president, and the commander-in-chief truly shape the war.
"I thanked Guido for his personal support and for offering me the opportunity to serve as his adviser on defense innovation. In this role, I will help Italy develop modern warfare technologies," he said.
Crozetto moved within a day
The Italian minister said he called Fedorov the day after the dismissal and asked when he would come to Rome to work as an advisor.
Fedorov met Crosetto on the first stop of an international trip focused on digitalization and defense technology.
The focus stays on his own projects
Fedorov said his main focus is unchanged and that he continues working in Ukraine on his own projects to strengthen its defense and attract international resources. In the advisory role, he will help Italy develop technologies of modern war and adapt to new security challenges, he wrote.
The two discussed drones, autonomous systems, air defense, and the development of a defense-tech ecosystem. The future of defense belongs to countries that can quickly test and scale new solutions, Fedorov said, and Ukraine's experience could serve as the basis for a new defense model for Europe.
Earlier, the Ukrainian parliament approved Yevhenii Khmara as the new defense minister. During his first speech, Khmara made it clear that he would continue his predecessor's course — the technologization of the army.
He added that there "would be more Ukrainian weapons, and strikes would be more precise.

articles.body:
The Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) said on Friday, Aug. 28, that they had completed the sixth cycle of a NATO-backed program aimed at strengthening the service members’ psychological resilience and restoring combat readiness.
The program, delivered under NATO’s Comprehensive Assistance Package for Ukraine, held 34 training seminars in July and August for more than 1,000 Ukrainian service members from different branches and categories, according to the General Staff.

“The seminars were not limited to the established training program; they also allowed for a rapid response to additional targeted requests from military-unit commanders,” the General Staff said in a statement.
NATO-backed activities
Overall coordination of NATO’s project activities is carried out by the Main Directorate for Psychological Support of Personnel of the AFU.
According to the General Staff, the directorate collects requests from military units and determines where practical seminars are needed.
The Officers’ League, a Ukrainian nongovernmental organization (NGO) that has worked on psychological support for the AFU personnel since 2014 carries out the project’s implementation.
Post-combat recovery
The training focused on strengthening the personnel’s psychological resilience, including developing self-help skills and the ability to help fellow soldiers in acute stress situations.
Constant exposure to violence and death has sharply increased the risk of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and other mental health conditions, including anxiety and depression, among both Ukrainian service members and civilians.

articles.title: Russian officer killed in St. Petersburg car bombing identified as Sergei Sechkov, whose unit Ukraine accuses of strikes on civilians
articles.body:
The person killed in the Aug. 27 car explosion in St. Petersburg has been identified as 43-year-old Russian serviceman Sergei Sechkov, according to Ukrainian Telegram channel Supernova+. Sechkov’s father confirmed to the independent outlet Agentstvo that his son had died in the bombing.
A number of known details about Sechkov match information about the victim that were previously reported by Russian media. According to 78.ru, the victim was a native of Ryazan named “Sergei S.,” and his wife, who was injured in the explosion, was named Anna. According to leaked data reviewed by Agentstvo, Sechkov was 43 years old, was born in Ryazan, and his wife’s name is Anna. In addition, Sechkov’s registered address is located roughly a hundred meters from the site of the explosion.
The Ukrainian project Myrotvorets has a profile for Sergei Sergeevich Sechkov on its website, listing him with the rank of major in military unit 12633 — the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment, part of the 6th Air Force and Air Defense Army. The St. Petersburg outlet Fontanka had previously written that the victim served in the Air Force and Air Defense troops, but referred to him as a lieutenant colonel.
In May 2022, Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) stated that servicemen of the 332nd Separate Guards Helicopter Regiment had taken part in the war against Ukraine. The HUR accused the unit of carrying out missile and bomb strikes on civilians in the Slobozhanske sector.
The car explosion in question took place on the morning of Aug. 27 near a store on Kolpinskoye Highway in the Slavyanka neighborhood of St. Petersburg. The serviceman inside the car was killed, and his wife was injured and hospitalized. The St. Petersburg office of the Investigative Committee confirmed the serviceman’s death and reported that a criminal case had been opened “over the car catching fire,” without specifying the charge.
Fontanka claims that a 24-year-old Russian woman planted the homemade explosive device under the car. According to the outlet’s account, on the evening of Aug. 26 she attached the device to the underside of the car beneath the driver’s seat, then headed to Pulkovo Airport and departed for Turkey at around five o’clock in the morning — a few hours before the explosion. Allegedly, she subsequently moved on to Chișinău, Moldova. The outlet does not name her or disclose the source of this information. Russian law enforcement agencies have not made any official statements about a search for a suspect.
The Ukrainian side has not confirmed involvement in the explosion, and no one has claimed responsibility for it.
Earlier, 78.ru reported that the victim had told his superiors he was “on a kill list.”

articles.title: Taiwan’s AI strategy has a public data problem
articles.body:
Taiwan Power Co (Taipower, 台電) chairman Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) uses a sports metaphor to describe the density of electricity demand. A household is a ping-pong ball, ordinary industry a baseball and a science park a bowling ball. A data center is a shot put.
Taiwan is preparing for the shot puts. Four new combined-cycle units at Hsinta (興達) and Taichung (台中), with combined capacity of about 5.2GW, are scheduled to begin supplying or testing on the grid by the end of this year. The Energy Administration’s (能源署) plan adds about 25.98GW of gas-fired capacity between this year and 2035, predominantly fueled by imported liquefied natural gas (LNG).
NUMBERS HARD TO FOLLOW
Photo: Reuters
The figures on the demand side are harder to follow. The government has released estimates for artificial intelligence data centers, but not the project-level information needed to match them with Taipower’s connection data. Power plants, LNG terminals and transmission lines endure for decades. The public record does not show how a request becomes an operating load, or whether the infrastructure is proportionate to the demand claimed.
Officials presenting the national electricity supply-and-demand report in June cited roughly 1.2GW of identified AI data-center demand within the 2035 planning horizon, plus a 2GW to 3GW allowance for faster growth. Taipower tells the Taipei Times that as of July 31, it had received 75 requests from “transmission-level data centers,” representing 4,523 megawatts (MW) of requested capacity. It had agreed to 47 requests totaling 3,331MW, but said about 40 percent of those cases did not proceed to a formal application within the deadline and expired.
The 4,523MW is not active demand, approved capacity, contracted capacity or an energized load. It is what applicants asked for at an earlier stage. Those are different claims on the power system.
TT file photo
Investigative outlet The Reporter (報導者) in April published Taipower data dated from November last year. It recorded 79 transmission-level requests totaling 4,758MW. Taipower had agreed to 40 cases totaling 3,033MW, but more than 70 percent of those cases had expired after the applicants did not initiate the formal application process within six months.
Both datasets might be accurate. They have different cutoff dates and might treat expired cases differently. No published note explains how they fit together.
Natalie Wong (王慧敏) of National Chengchi University tells the Taipei Times that she tried to put them in order. She could not reconcile Taipower’s data with the 1.2GW cited by officials in June and the 303.5 megawatts (MW) known to have been physically connected. The last number is the only one tied to operating infrastructure. Taiwan therefore has several measures of data-center demand, with no public rule for choosing among them.
The 303.5MW is the contracted capacity of four sites receiving power, not their measured consumption. Five more sites were under construction with 567MW of approved supply capacity. These figures are closer to real projects, but still say nothing about hourly use.
Taipower has published an AI estimate before. An August 2024 presentation gave annual figures through 2030, including data centers, and briefly described the method. The Taipei Times could not locate subsequently published annual AI data using the same format.
The June report folded AI data centers and semiconductor expansion into national demand growth of 2.5 percent a year through 2035.
The Energy Administration told the Taipei Times that its forecast draws on applications from AI data centers and semiconductor companies, adjusted for past consumption and efficiency. Its reply did not provide current numbers for AI.
Tseng has separately estimated that semiconductor electricity use could rise from 52 billion kilowatt-hours this year to 110 billion in 2035, approaching 30 percent of national consumption. As of press time, no comparable data is currently available to the public for AI data centers.
Forecasts change. Projects fail, and applicants reserve capacity they never use. That uncertainty is not the problem; keeping its effects out of view is. Outsiders cannot see which assumptions changed or what those changes mean for power plants, terminals and grid reinforcement.
ENERGY SOURCES
Gas generated 47.8 percent of Taiwan’s electricity last year. New units are replacing retiring coal capacity and generation lost after the Ma-anshan Nuclear Power Plant in Pingtung County’s Hengchun Township (恆春) ceased generating in May last year and entered the decommissioning process. If data center and semiconductor demand exceeds the national forecast, Taiwan must burn more gas, accelerate other generation or reduce demand elsewhere.
Taiwan has no international gas pipeline; all of its natural-gas imports arrive as LNG by sea. Tsai-ying Lu (呂采穎), who directs the energy security and climate resilience program at the Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology (DSET, 科技、民主與社會研究中心), said her team is researching Taiwan’s energy security under contingency. That work also needs the size, location and hourly profile of new loads. Neither Taipower nor the Energy Administration appears to publish a current aggregate hourly load profile specifically for AI data centers.
Hydrogen is not yet a commercial alternative. Taipower and Academia Sinica completed a short 10 percent blending test using a 65kW microturbine in 2023. A draft government plan calls for a one-hour demonstration at a 20 percent hydrogen blend in a roughly 5MW system in 2028, but gives no timetable for supplying power stations. Asked how Taiwan would avoid prolonged dependence on LNG, the Energy Administration cited solar, offshore wind and geothermal. Those sources can reduce how often gas units run, but they do not provide a non-LNG fuel for the gas fleet itself.
Geothermal capacity remains below 14MW. Alexander Helling, chief executive of Baseload Capital, a geothermal developer whose Google-backed Taiwan projects aim to add 10MW by 2029, said drilling risk and slow permitting keep projects difficult to finance.
Data centers are concentrated in the north, while much of Taiwan’s generation is farther south. Taipower has encouraged large technology projects to locate closer to generation and in municipalities that support new power infrastructure. The logic is clear enough. The data behind individual siting decisions remain largely internal.
‘ENERGY USAGE STATEMENT’
Under Article 16 of the Energy Management Act (能源管理法), and rules amended in October and November last year, a new or expanded hyperscale or colocation data center planning energy-use capacity of at least 5MW must prepare an “energy usage statement”. The authority handling its permit forwards the statement to the Ministry of Economic Affairs. The review covers efficiency and, under a proposed amendment, industrial benefits. It does not open the connection queue or the demand model used for generation and transmission planning.
In Taoyuan’s Gueishan District (龜山), a resident told The Reporter that locals learned only after construction began that the project was related to AI. Municipal planners cannot plan coherently if they do not know which electricity requests are speculative, agreed, expired or likely to become operating loads.
Wong used the term “deservingness” for this bargain. A city gains electricity and investment by accepting the infrastructure that supplies them. Communities are asked to host infrastructure for a national policy whose demand forecast is not available at that level of detail.
Taipower already holds most of the information needed to clear this up. An anonymized connection queue could show, by municipality and substation area, capacity requested, agreed, expired, contracted and energized. Preliminary requests could be separated from firm commitments without naming customers. The Energy Administration could publish a current range for AI demand, its assumptions and the effects on gas consumption and grid construction.
Taiwan may decide that greater reliance on imported gas is an acceptable price for its AI and semiconductor ambitions. Publishing the underlying data would not settle that choice. It would allow lawmakers, municipalities and host communities to test the same assumptions as the ministries making them.
Romain Blachier is president of Association France-Formosa and an associate fellow at the Fondation Jean-Jaures. He works in renewable energy, consults and teaches energy geopolitics.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: The objective is one thousand drones for long-range strikes against Russia per day

Zelenskyy: The objective is one thousand drones for long-range strikes against Russia per day
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy stated the goal of one thousand long-range drones per day. According to him, the strikes have already restricted the movement of vessels in Novorossiysk.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy held a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief, following which he said that Ukraine’s task is to deploy one thousand drones for long-range strikes per day against Russia, UNN reports.
"Today I held a meeting of the Staff. The key thing is to maximize our weapons for protection against Russian strikes on Ukraine. The main thing is our defense against jet-powered "Shaheds" and making our deep strikes against Russia even more frequent. The task is one thousand drones for long-range strikes per day against Russia. At present, we have an average of 300-plus long-range strikes, and there must be more. There is a very specific goal, and we will accomplish this task," Zelenskyy said.
He noted that the Russians had chosen a tactic of intensifying terror: constant air-raid alerts one after another in Kyiv, with jet-powered "Shaheds" unfortunately flying in.
"The same is happening in our other cities and communities—constant strikes on Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia. Sumy region, Chernihiv region, Dnipropetrovsk region, our Kherson. Ordinary civilian enterprises were damaged in Kyiv region. All, all our countermeasures are already being used, and it is important to significantly accelerate the production of interceptors specifically against such jet-powered "Shaheds", so that our deep strikes give Russia a greater sense of its responsibility for choosing to continue this war," Zelenskyy added.
According to him, peace could have been achieved long ago, but the only person who is not interested in peace rules in Moscow.
"They already have less gasoline, less exports, and less logistics. For the first time in its history, Russia is importing gasoline and is effectively spending budget funds to support oil companies. And they will suffer even greater losses if Russia does not want to talk properly about ending this war. There were also reports from our military regarding Novorossiysk: we are already achieving our result—no vessel is entering or leaving their Novorossiysk port. And each such day without movement in Novorossiysk contributes to reducing Russia’s war potential. We will certainly find ways to block their other ports as well. We did not start this war, and we are entirely justified in responding to Russian actions," the President noted.
Let us recall
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reported receiving a report from the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, as well as an update on Russia’s production of ballistic missiles and plans to scale up this production, stating that there would be a response.

articles.title: Warsaw wants nuclear deterrence, but without nukes
articles.body:
Warsaw wants nuclear deterrence, but without nukes
Poland has sent confusing signals regarding the potential deployment of nuclear weaponry on its territory, in what appears to be an attempt to enjoy the fruits of deterrence without hosting foreign munitions.
In recent months, a dozen European NATO members, including Poland, have expressed a desire to either host nuclear weapons or take part in nuclear-sharing initiatives to varying degrees. Apart from existing nuclear sharing within the bloc, which involves hosting US munitions, France has proposed an EU-focused scheme to deploy its own weapons to willing nations.
The confusion began on Thursday, when Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski appeared to rule out ever hosting the weaponry on the country’s soil.
“I would like to say very clearly and openly: Poland does not want to have nuclear warheads on its territory,” Zalewski told reporters at NATO headquarters in Brussels. “We want to participate in NATO nuclear deterrence, [which] does not mean to have a nuclear warhead on our territory.”
The remarks caused quite a stir, with some interpreting it as a refusal to participate in the proposed European or even existing NATO nuclear-sharing schemes. The confusion prompted Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz to step in and assure the public that Warsaw still wants to participate in nuclear sharing.
“To dispel any doubts: Poland remains steadfastly interested in participating in the NATO Nuclear Sharing program. We are also conducting talks regarding the proposal for participation in the European nuclear protective umbrella. Our government’s stance on these issues is unequivocal,” he wrote on X.
While the minister did not explicitly say whether Warsaw was open to hosting foreign nukes, Zalewski doubled down on his original remarks later in the day. Poland remains committed to participating in “NATO’s nuclear deterrence, [but] without storing nuclear weapons,” the official wrote on X while berating those confused by his statements. “Security requires competence and seriousness. Claiming that Nuclear Sharing [equates to] storing nuclear weapons in Poland is ignorance or deliberate manipulation,” he asserted.

articles.title: Zelensky orders Ukraine’s military to launch 1,000 drones a day at Russia
articles.body:
Zelensky orders Ukraine’s military to launch 1,000 drones a day at Russia
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he ordered Ukraine’s military to launch 1,000 drones a day at Russia.
Today I held a meeting of the Staff. The key task is to maximize production of our weapons to defend against Russian strikes on Ukraine. The main thing is our defense against jet-powered Shaheds and making our long-range strikes on Russia even more frequent. The task is 1,000 drones a day for long-range sanctions against Russia. Right now, we’re averaging more than 300 a day — that number needs to grow.
Zelensky said that “the goal is very specific” and that Ukraine “will fulfill this task.”
In early July, Zelensky told the Financial Times that the war’s key phase had shifted from land and sea to the air, calling the “battle in the sky” the deciding factor in the conflict’s outcome. “When it is no longer one hundred drones but one thousand flying toward Moscow… he [Vladimir Putin] will understand,” Zelensky said. “Once he begins to feel it personally, once he begins to see it with his own eyes, you will see advisers urging him to relocate somewhere beyond the Urals. The farther Putin is from Moscow, the closer the end of the war will be.”

articles.title: Italy’s Crosetto Appoints Fedorov as Defense Innovation Adviser
articles.body:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has accepted Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto’s invitation to serve as an adviser on defense innovation.
Fedorov announced his new role on Friday, Aug. 28, in a statement posted to Telegram, unveiling that he had met with Crosetto during the first stop of an international trip focused on digitalization and defense-technology projects.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Ukraine’s experience can become the foundation for a new European defense model,” Fedorov said, adding that “the future of defense belongs to countries able to quickly test and scale new solutions, combining technology with strong manufacturing.”
Continuing support for Ukraine projects
Fedorov said his main focus would remain Ukraine, where he will continue working on projects intended to reinforce the country’s defenses and attract international resources.
He was ousted as defense minister on July 15 as part as part of President Volodymyr Zelensky’s broader cabinet reshuffle, and was replaced by Yevhen Khmara – a former major general of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) who has spent most of his career in special operations.
The move triggered major protests nationwide throughout July, with demonstrators calling for Fedorov to be reinstated.
Italy’s diplomatic stance on the war in Ukraine
On June 19, Crosetto said Italy would not contribute funds to NATO’s Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), which finances purchases of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
Ukraine Needs 30,000 Monthly Mobilizations, Budanov Says
He said Rome opposed the mechanism but maintained that other channels could provide Ukraine with the needed military support.
“We have said no from the beginning, and it is still a no,” Crosetto said, despite last year’s announcement that Rome was warming up to the idea of taking part in PURL.
Italy has also pushed back on some of the EU’s sanctions on Russia.
On June 25, Rome and Paris raised concerns over an EU proposal to bar former Russian combatants from entering the bloc, arguing that the issue could be handled through visa policy rather than sanctions.
On July 3, Italy joined Bulgaria in objecting to EU plans to impose a visa ban on Russian Orthodox Patriarch Kirill, a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.
According to Politico, citing three anonymous EU diplomats, Rome’s concerns stemmed partly from the Vatican and centered mainly on unease about sanctioning the leader of a Christian denomination.
Crosetto has consistently ruled out deploying Italian troops to Ukraine as well, saying that direct military intervention would risk escalating the conflict.
At the same time, he has said Italy supports assisting Ukraine “in every possible way” short of sending its forces into the country.

articles.title: MP questions Royal Navy support for Irish defence summit
articles.body:
A Conservative MP has questioned the use of Royal Navy assets to support security arrangements around an informal meeting of European defence ministers in Ireland, arguing that restrictions associated with Irish neutrality could limit the usefulness of any British deployment, the UK Defence Journal understands.
John Cooper, MP for Dumfries and Galloway, raised the issue in a letter dated 28 August to Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, after reports that Dublin had requested Royal Navy support for the meeting in Wicklow.
Cooper wrote: “I am aghast at media reports from Dublin that their Government has requested support from the Royal Navy for security, but that any vessel involved must stay outside their 12-mile territorial-waters limit.”
In a social media post accompanying the letter, he said: “Neutral Ireland portrays their gunboat George Bernard Shaw protecting an EU defence event there next week… but they’ve asked for help from the Royal Navy… who must get close enough to be much use! I’ve asked the Defence Secretary why we’re paying for this idiocy.”
The meeting is due to take place in Wicklow as Ireland holds the rotating presidency of the European Union. Cooper’s letter asks whether the Defence Secretary will attend and whether the UK will reconsider the deployment of British forces in support of the event.
He linked his concerns to a reported incident near Dublin Airport in December, when uncrewed aerial vehicles were detected close to the airport as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy arrived.
Cooper wrote: “While the Irish Defence Forces spotted the UAVs, they had no ability to interdict, lacking any meaningful air-to-air or surface-to-air capability.”
He acknowledged that Ireland possesses a small number of RBS Bolide short-range air-defence missiles, but argued that these would provide only limited coverage against fast-moving or higher-altitude threats.
The MP also questioned the value of positioning foreign warships outside Irish territorial waters. He wrote: “This insistence that foreign warships remain outside Irish limits hampers their effectiveness. The Royal Navy is being asked to do a bad job. To add insult to injury, British taxpayers are footing the bill for this bodge.”
Cooper went on to argue that Ireland’s long-standing policy of military neutrality has not been matched by sufficient investment in its own defence capabilities, despite recent moves to increase spending.
He said: “The Republic makes great play of its neutrality but has for too long not funded this in the way that, for example, Switzerland does.”
The letter also refers to expected French involvement in security arrangements around the Wicklow meeting. Cooper said the French frigate Aquitaine was expected to remain 12 miles from the Irish coast and questioned how useful its air-defence missile system would be from that position against small or fast uncrewed aircraft.
He wrote: “Her Aster surface-to-air missiles will have the range to cover Carlow, but against low and fast UAVs may be a sledgehammer when a scalpel is required.”
Cooper suggested that smaller-calibre naval weapons might be more suitable against some uncrewed aerial threats, adding that foreign ships would still have to be positioned sufficiently close to be effective.
The MP also raised the broader question of military cooperation between Britain and Ireland, asking the Defence Secretary whether the UK should reconsider the current relationship.
He wrote: “Will you look again at the deployment of any British forces for this ‘informal’ chit-chat next week? It is both an affront to Britain and unaffordable expense, especially when our involvement is subject to damaging caveats?”
Cooper then asked: “More substantially, will you bring to the House details of a reset of our military relations with Ireland?”
The letter ends with a broader criticism of Ireland’s defence posture and the degree to which British forces might be expected to assist during an emergency.
Cooper wrote: “We can no longer afford to let the Irish walk on our cane. Will the Marine Nationale bear the cost of protecting those cables and pipelines? Do you agree that rather than RAF Typhoons and F-35 Lightning IIs scrambling – at gulping expense – to intercept anything airborne in the Republic’s airspace, it should be over to the Armée de l’air et de l’espace to cover IDF blushes?”
He concluded: “Ireland must accept neutrality without funding is simply freeloading.”

articles.title: Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people per month, Budanov says, warns war won't end soon
articles.body:
Ukraine must mobilize at least 30,000 people per month, Budanov says, warns war won't end soon
Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov has warned that Ukraine cannot afford to mobilize less than 30,000 people per month, as ending the war in the short term is "unrealistic."
The comments, made on Aug. 28 on Ukrainian television, come as Ukraine's leadership is under increasing pressure from both the military and society to tackle issues in the country's flawed and unpopular mobilization process.
Forced mobilization, as a part of martial law, has been in place in Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion began in February 2022.
Since the draft ramped up in scope over last years as less Ukrainians volunteered to fight, mobilization has been a source of simmering tension in Ukrainian society. Cases of attacks on draft officers increased in frequency over 2026.
Aware of the topic's political sensitivity, Ukraine's leadership, from parliament, the defense ministry, and President Zelensky himself, have consistently avoided taking public responsibility for comprehensively reforming the draft.
But Ukraine requires a consistent flow of new recruits to stay in the fight, with Moscow showing no signs of stopping its war and increasing signs that a new mobilization wave in Russia could follow State Duma elections in autumn.
"No matter how much we say that we will call differently now, the quantitative indicators will not change, which means that the number of dissatisfied people will not change either," said Budanov.
"You can't do anything about it."
In the interview, Budanov also urged Ukrainians not to believe that an end to the war could be around the corner.
"I think very soon everyone will see negotiations, but it will be more about the technical side and preparation for something big, which I hope we will get to someday," he said.
"We will not stop the war now. Not because we don't want to, it's just not realistic."
On Aug. 22, parliamentary defense committee secretary Roman Kostenko said Ukraine is preparing "radical" changes to its mobilization system, including potential revisions to the country's draft age.
Kostenko said financial incentives to encourage Ukrainians to sign military contracts have failed to significantly increase recruitment, prompting officials to consider other measures.
Budanov, who had served as the popular leader of Ukraine's military intelligence agency HUR, was appointed Presidential Office head after his predecessor Andrii Yermak was searched by anti-corruption agencies.
Now, the former general has himself come under scrutiny, after Ukrainian media revealed on Aug. 26 that Budanov's name and voice featured prominently in audio tapes recorded by investigators for the case around his deputy Iryna Mudra, who was charged — and promptly dismissed — by President Zelensky.
“Let the court sort it out," Budanov said in response to his mentioning in the tapes. "You know, it (his name) comes up in a lot of places,” Budanov said when asked about alleged references to him in the tapes.
