articles.title: Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
articles.body:
This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: August 28, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
As we tally Russian losses, we are trying to determine the military ranks of those killed, and we are maintaining a separate list of officers with the rank of lieutenant colonel and above.
On March 31, an An-26 aircraft carrying the staff of the Northern Fleet’s Air Corps crashed in Crimea. Since then, the authorities have officially confirmed the death of only one officer: Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko.
Mediazona strives to track specific events of this war, such as the sinking of the cruiser Moskva or the mass deaths of conscripts on New Year’s Eve 2022/2023. We expected that a list of those killed in the plane crash in Crimea would be officially published or that a memorial dedicated to the victims of this accident would be erected. As far as we know, this has not happened.
Nevertheless, we have managed to identify 27 names of military personnel who are presumed to have died in the An-26 crash. You can read the full list here:
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By August 28, 2026, the death of 7,596 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 225,000 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 228,450 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

articles.title: The KMT’s failed ‘Taiwanization’
articles.body:
The “quiet revolution” of Taiwan’s democratization took shape during the 12 years that followed Lee Teng-hui (李登輝) simultaneously becoming chairman of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and president of the Republic of China (ROC). Chen Shui-bian (陳水扁) of the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) then took the presidential helm in 2000, bringing an end to one-party rule in the ROC, and was re-elected in 2004. He was followed by the KMT’s Ma Ying-jeou (馬英九), who served two four-year terms; the DPP’s Tsai Ing-wen (蔡英文), who also served two terms; and the DPP’s William Lai (賴清德), currently in his first term. Having won just three presidential elections to the DPP’s five, the KMT finds itself gripped by anxiety over its ability to govern the country. The predicament goes back to Ma cementing the KMT’s abandonment of Lee’s political project of Taiwanese localization.
Lee’s politics, which elements within the KMT still steeped in colonial conceptions of Chinese identity labelled as pro-independence, in fact were for a practical localization, or “Taiwanization” of the ROC. This embodied a political realism regarding the ROC’s development in place. Lee also sought to reform the KMT, to cure its colonial hangover, and free it from the confines of party-state ideology. Perhaps this was his way of repaying former president Chiang Ching-kuo (蔣經國), who appointed Lee as vice president in 1984. Chiang and his father and predecessor, Chiang Kai-shek (蔣介石), were fully taken with colonial ideations of Chinese identity. Chiang Ching-kuo’s passing in 1988 presented Lee with the opportunity to make that shift. What remained of “China” in the republic was to be reborn locally as Taiwan.
Like Lee, former Taiwan provincial governor Lin Yang-kang (林洋港) and former vice premier Chiu Chuang-han (邱創煥) were also potential contenders to succeed Chiang Ching-kuo as president. However, they were the epitome of local politickers and bureaucrats; their knowledge and education was confined to navigating the party-state system, and they lacked a broad and ambitious political vision. After Lee assumed the presidency and amid the turmoil of the post-Chiang era, Lin teamed up with the former premier Hau Pei-tsun (郝柏村) to mount an independent challenge in the 1996 presidential election. Former Control Yuan president Chen Li-an (陳履安) did the same with his then-running mate, lawyer Wang Ching-feng (王清峰). Their two tickets won a combined vote share of no more than 25 percent, far behind the 75 percent won collectively by Lee with then-premier Lien Chan (連戰) and the DPP’s Peng Ming-min (彭明敏) with Frank Hsieh (彭明敏). At the time, the Taiwanization of the KMT complemented the DPP.
In the 2000 presidential election, Lien was the KMT’s presidential candidate, but the KMT vote split when former governor James Soong (宋楚瑜) entered the race as an independent, winning more votes than Lien and resulting in the DPP’s Chen Shui-bian taking the presidency. Lien and Soong then ran together in 2004, but lost to Chen Shui-bian once again. Lien not only turned his back on Lee, but abandoned Taiwan in favor of China and reversed the Taiwanese identity that he had previously embraced, at least nominally, under Lee’s influence. This marked a major setback for the localization of the KMT. Then came Ma, under whose rule the KMT’s Chinese self-conceptualization as an exiled colony became even more deeply entrenched. This road, it seems, has been one of no return.
Lee’s direct challenges within the KMT began with the first direct election for Taipei mayor in 1994. Jaw Shaw-kong (趙少康) left the KMT to run against the party’s nominee and mayoral incumbent Huang Ta-chou (黃大洲), splitting the vote and allowing DPP candidate Chen Shui-bian to win. At the time, Jaw was a KMT figure on the far right and proponent of the party’s Chinese identity. He loudly and publicly warned that Taiwan faced national annihilation, forming the New KMT Alliance faction in late 1989 to challenge Lee’s localization program. The faction ultimately broke away to establish the New Party in 1993. Meanwhile, KMT members who supported Lee’s approach and hoped for a KMT rooted in Taiwan had formed the pro-localization Collective Wisdom Club faction in 1988, and the Taiwan Solidarity Union was established in 2001. However, after Lee’s death, no Taiwanese localization force emerged from outside the DPP.
After the KMT established its rule in Taiwan in the immediate post-war period, large numbers of Taiwanese elites were eliminated in the 228 Incident, and some local gentry aligned themselves with the regime in its early years. Native Taiwanese political forces within the party-state system came to consist roughly of two groups: one made up of civil servants from the education sector and the China Youth Corps, who mainly became mayors and county commissioners or senior government officials; the other being local councilors and representatives widely regarded as being controlled by organized crime. This was fundamentally different from the DPP, which emerged from the dangwai (黨外, “outside the party”) movement, carried a reformist character, and won broad public support.
The reconvening of two forces — those with a “colonizer syndrome” and strong ideological fixations, and the “colonized syndrome” sufferers driven largely by self-interest within the systems that be — took shape as the DPP moved toward a position of stable political dominance. The KMT ticket for the 2024 presidential election embodied this reconvening, with Jaw, representing the former, serving as the running mate of New Taipei City Mayor Hou You-yi (侯友宜), representing the latter. The KMT’s predicament can be summed up like this: It has chosen to draw on the very Chinese Communist Party forces that forced it into exile in Taiwan in the first place, rather than becoming Taiwan’s own national party and jointly building a new state. The KMT’s failed Taiwanization is a shadow hanging over Taiwan’s quiet revolution, and the unfinished reality of Lee’s political vision.

articles.title: Wilsbach Meets with Top Israeli Military Leaders in Middle East Visit
articles.body:
U.S. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach visited Israel in recent days as the conflict with Iran hit six months, meeting with the heads of the Israel Defense Forces and the Israeli Air Force.
Wilsbach’s meeting with top Israeli military leaders Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir and Maj. Gen. Omer Tischler took place Aug. 23, the IDF announced Aug. 26. Wilsbach confirmed the meeting in an Aug. 28 social media post.
The IDF said the leaders discussed “the regional situation, advancing learning from the joint campaign, and future areas of cooperation.” Wilsbach wrote that they talked over “shared priorities for regional security [and] opportunities to deepen cooperation.”
The U.S. Air Force has yet to release a readout from the meeting, and a USAF spokesperson did not immediately respond to a query from Air & Space Forces Magazine.
The visit is Wilsbach’s first publicized visit to the Middle East since the start of the Iran war, which began Feb. 28 with dual air campaigns named Operation Epic Fury and Operation Roaring Lion.
Over the course of the past six months, the U.S. and Israel have struck thousands of Iranian targets for the largest air campaign in the Middle East in a generation. During that time, the USAF has stationed fighter jets and aerial refuelers at Israeli airports and air bases.
The monthslong presence of KC-46 and KC-135 tankers at Ben Gurion International Airport near Tel Aviv, has tested the capacity of Israel’s main commercial airport. In July, Israeli officials said they would limit the number of USAF aircraft that could stay there so as to not disrupt commercial travel.
Since the most recent flareup in mid-to-late July, combat operations against Iran have slowed, with U.S. forces focusing on enforcing a blockade of Iranian ships and ports. President Donald Trump’s administration has instead focused more on inflicting economic pressure on Iran.
Still, the Pentagon is maintaining a large force posture in the region under U.S. Central Command, including dozens of USAF aircraft.
Wilsbach previously visited the CENTCOM area of responsibility in December 2025 as part of a major trip to seven bases in the Middle East and Europe. In July, he visited London for the Global Air and Space Chiefs Conference, RAF Mildenhall in the U.K., and Aviano Air Base in Italy.

articles.title: Ukraine prepares to ease residency rules for foreign fighters
articles.body:
Ukraine's government approved a draft law that aims to give foreign and stateless nationals who served in the Ukrainian military more time to formalize their residency status after the end of their contract, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Aug. 28 on Telegram.
The draft law aims to extend the legal temporary residence period in Ukraine after completion of military service from three to six months, according to the Prime Minister.
Time spent serving in the armed forces will count toward the five year residency requirement for the immigration permit, Koretskyi said.
A law passed by Ukraine's Parliament on June 18, 2025, reduced the necessary contract service time for foreign fighters to apply for citizenship from three years to one.
A special certificate will also be introduced for those foreigners who cannot travel abroad to obtain or exchange a passport in their country of origin due to threats or political circumstances, Koretskyi announced.
This is especially relevant to volunteers from Belarus and Russia, who face criminal prosecution in their countries of origin.
Many fighters from the Freedom for Russia Legion or the Kastus Kalinowski regiment have received awards from the state, while their legal status in the country remains under question.
Decree No. 110/2026, introduced on Feb. 11, allows applicants for Ukrainian citizenship to file an application to renounce their previous citizenship instead of having them formally exit it, which for some would require returning to their countries of origin. The decree also allowed to apply for citizenship on an expired passport.
Currently, the law only allows for the application of citizenship and sets no obligation on the state to decide within an official time frame.
Since even before the full-scale invasion, Ukraine's State Migration Service has had a reputation for taking a long time to decide on the naturalization of foreigners.
The new draft law now needs approval from Ukraine's Parliament. The bill has not yet been registered.
On June 12, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a fresh drive to recruit foreign fighters, with then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov saying that Kyiv aimed for 30-50% of the army's infantry and assault troops to be made up of foreigners.
Foreign fighters, especially those from Latin America, continue to play an increasing role in the Ukrainian army, often carrying out the very same unenviable infantry and assault missions.
The changes come amid Ukraine's chronic manpower crisis, with many personnel exhausted after years of full-scale war without a path for demobilization and discharge, while newly-mobilized soldiers tend to be increasingly unmotivated, especially in the infantry.

articles.title: Russia has destroyed 90% of Ukraine’s modern commercial storage capacity. Retail logistics are being reshaped
articles.body:
Russian attacks have destroyed about 90% of Ukraine’s modern facilities for storing goods, significantly disrupting the country’s retail logistics, Ukraine’s Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said on 28 August, according to Interfax-Ukraine.
Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine’s civilian commercial and logistics infrastructure in recent weeks, striking warehouses, distribution centers, hypermarkets, postal terminals and other facilities that keep goods moving through the country. The campaign has damaged supply chains and forced businesses to find more expensive and vulnerable ways to store and deliver products.
Vysotskyi said the destruction does not pose a threat of famine, but warned that continued Russian attacks on logistics infrastructure could affect the range of products available in Ukrainian stores. Supermarkets in Kyiv have already seen widespread empty shelves in recent weeks.
Retailers forced to change how goods are delivered
The destruction of warehouses has forced retailers to change how they move products around the country, with deliveries increasingly being made “from the wheels” rather than through conventional storage and distribution facilities, Vysotskyi said.
Such logistics are more complicated and expensive, he said, while some companies have begun relocating their operations to other areas. Russian attacks, however, have also reached some of the relocated facilities.
The comments come as Russia has increasingly targeted commercial and logistics infrastructure across Ukraine. In recent days, Russian drones have struck warehouses, hypermarkets, postal terminals and shopping centers, including in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia.
Kyiv has been under attack for 2 days nonstop. Russia is targeting the capital’s civilian supply chains
No threat of famine, minister says
Despite the scale of the destruction, Vysotskyi stressed that Ukraine does not face a food shortage severe enough to threaten the population with famine.
The main impact is expected to be on logistics, availability and the range of goods offered in stores. With fewer storage facilities, retailers have less capacity to stock products and must rely more heavily on direct deliveries.
The shift can also increase costs because goods have to move more frequently and over potentially longer routes without the buffer provided by large distribution centers.
Calls for risk-sharing after Russian strikes
Vysotskyi also called for a system to distribute the financial risks when Russian attacks destroy goods somewhere along the supply chain.
He said these losses currently fall within private contractual relationships between businesses, with the state not acting as an operator in the supply chain. In his view, the risks should be shared more fairly between companies involved in supplying and selling products.
He said such a system would not necessarily mean splitting losses equally. Different products have different margins, sales conditions and profitability, so the share of risk should depend on the specific product and terms of cooperation.
Russia’s attacks on storage and distribution infrastructure are therefore creating effects far beyond the facilities themselves. Damage to the supply chain can change what products reach stores, increase the cost of getting them there, and make Ukraine’s retail system more vulnerable to further strikes.

Mykhailo Fedorov, fired as Ukraine’s defense minister, agrees to become an advisor to Italy’s Guido Crosetto, but says his focus stays on Ukraine
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov met with Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto and thanked him for his support and for the offer to serve as an advisor on defense innovation.
“In this role, I will assist Italy in adopting modern warfare technologies, enhancing its defense sector, and adapting to emerging global security challenges,” he said in a social media post.
But Fedorov said his main focus remains unchanged. “I continue my work in Ukraine on core projects that strengthen our defense and help attract international resources,” he said.
Fedorov served as Ukraine’s defense minister from January to July 2026, when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky fired him, reportedly over a conflict with Ukrainian Armed Forces Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi. Crosetto reached out to Fedorov shortly afterward. “I called him the day after his dismissal and said, ‘When do you want to come to Rome and work with me as an advisor?’” he said.

articles.title: Zelenskiy says US gave Kyiv information about meetings in Moscow
articles.body:
Zelenskiy says US gave Kyiv information about meetings in Moscow
Aug 28 - Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Friday that the United States had given Kyiv information about a number of meetings in Moscow over the last few days.
"Today we received information from the American side about the meetings in Moscow that took place these days. There were a number of meetings there," Zelenskiy said on Telegram, without going into detail on who was at the meetings.
"I thank them for the information and for the necessary tone of the conversation with Russia," Zelenskiy added, again without elaborating.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had travelled to Moscow to warn Russia off any attack on a NATO member.
The Kremlin dismissed the report, while U.S. President Donald Trump said Russian President Vladimir Putin would not attack a NATO country, playing down media reports on Ratcliffe's trip.
Two sources told Reuters that Ratcliffe had raised the possibility of a Russian operation against a NATO member during the meeting, although it was unclear whether that was the primary purpose of the trip. The talks also covered Russia's support for Iran, one source told Reuters.
Also Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Friday that Warsaw was in constant contact with the CIA leadership and was not surprised by Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow.
"We are not taken by surprise by any information regarding the operations and initiatives the CIA Director is conducting," Tusk told a youth conference when asked if the visit should be a source of concern.
"Poland was also informed about the need for an urgent discussion on this matter at the highest possible Polish-American level," Tusk added without elaborating.
He said that there have been signals in the public domain that Russia is preparing to escalate tensions, both in the war with Ukraine and across the region, and that this autumn and winter are set to be pivotal for Russia. REUTERS

articles.title: As Iran Threatens Radio Farda And Other Media, US Points To Tehran's Record Of Targeting Journalists
articles.body:
WASHINGTON -- The United States said it was aware of threats by Iran's armed forces to put Persian-language media outlets including RFE/RL's Radio Farda on a list of potential military targets, and pointed to what it said was Tehran's record of harassment and attempted attacks against journalists and dissidents abroad.
In an August 28 response to a query from RFE/RL, a State Department spokesperson said, "We are aware of these reports."
"The Iranian regime has repeatedly harassed and attempted to kidnap and kill journalists and Iranian dissidents worldwide simply for exercising their freedoms. This is longstanding, despicable behavior from a regime that has propagated terror globally for decades," the spokesperson said.
"The United States stands with innocent civilians targeted by Iran and continues working with allies and partners to expose these threats, share threat information, and hold perpetrators accountable," the spokesperson continued.
In a televised interview earlier this week, Iranian armed forces spokesman Brigadier General Abolfazl Shekarchi named Radio Farda, Iran International, BBC Persian, and Manoto, and said their employees could be included in Iran's "bank of military targets." He called them "soldiers of Zionism and criminal America" and claimed, without providing evidence, that the outlets were connected variously to the CIA, Mossad, and other foreign intelligence services.
David Kramer, executive director of the George W. Bush Institute and a former US assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights, and labor, said Tehran's warning reflected the importance of the media outlets it said could be targeted.
"It's not a surprise that the Iranian regime would view outlets like Radio Farda and BBC Persian-language service as threats, since they don't want the Iranian people to know what's really happening," Kramer told RFE/RL.
"The regime's reaction shows that these services have a real impact inside Iran, whereas the regime prefers to operate through silence and violence against its own people and its neighbors," he said.
Radio Farda is the Iranian service of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), which says its mission is to "promote democratic values by providing accurate, uncensored news and open debate in countries where a free press is threatened and disinformation is pervasive."
Kramer said the media outlets "must be protected to be able to do their important work in advancing the interests of the American people through soft power, while also letting the Iranian people know they are not forgotten."
The Czech Republic, which hosts RFE/RL and Radio Farda in Prague, has protested the threats. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka said he was summoning the Iranian ambassador to appear at the ministry over the matter, Czech media reported.
"Radio Farda, based in Prague, has been one of the few channels getting verified information to the Iranian population. Its importance was especially clear during the mass repression which the Iranian regime subjected its people to in the winter," Czech Foreign Ministry spokesman Adam Corgo told Czech Radio.
He was referring to a deadly crackdown on nationwide protests in Iran in January. Foreign-based Iranian rights groups say they have verified around 7,000 deaths but that the real death toll is likely higher.
Thomas Melia, a former senior State Department official focusing on human rights and now a senior fellow at Georgetown University's Center for Democracy and Civil Society, said the threat should be taken seriously. He said Radio Farda personnel in Prague and elsewhere "need to heighten their security awareness," pointing to the Iranian state's actions targeting dissidents abroad.
Melia also said Tehran's threat underscored the importance of Radio Farda's work.
"It's a sign of how important the work of Farda is, that the Iranian regime is unhappy that the true facts and information and news reports that Farda broadcasts are getting to the Iranian people, and they want to cut that off," Melia said.
Christopher Walker, vice president of the Washington-based Center for European Policy Analysis, said Iran takes the competition over information seriously and has invested heavily in its state information capabilities.
"The Iranian authorities take media and information competition very seriously," Walker said. "It's why they are understood to spend hundreds of millions of dollars annually on their state information capabilities around the world."
Walker described the threats against international Persian-language outlets and other independent sources as part of what he called Tehran's "longstanding pattern of transnational censorship and repression."
He also placed the Iranian threats within a broader confrontation over information between authoritarian governments and Western democracies.
"This is part of a global shadow war being waged on the West by regimes in Moscow, Beijing, as well as Tehran," Walker said, to which "free countries need a far more cohesive and determined response."
Retired Vice Admiral Robert Harward, a former deputy commander of US Central Command, said Iran's hostility toward independent media was rooted in the nature of the clerical authorities who have held power since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
"At its core, the regime has always been against free press and anybody willing to speak, and they've been able to control that internally," Harward told RFE/RL. "Now, as they get more desperate, they're going to go after all the external pressure because it tells the truth about what a despotic regime it is," he said.
RFE/RL reports in 24 languages to 18 countries. It is a private, nonprofit American media corporation funded by a grant from the US Congress through the United States Agency for Global Media.

articles.title: Ukrainian ex-Defense Minister Fedorov becomes adviser to Italian official
articles.body:
Ukrainian ex-Minister Fedorov becomes adviser to Italian official, plans to visit US
Ukrainian ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has agreed to become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto during a visit to Rome, Fedorov’s press service told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 28.
He is planning to visit the United States next in order to "secure resources for new defense tech projects," Fedorov's press service said.
Fedorov served as defense minister from January to July and was widely seen as highly effective.
President Volodymyr Zelensky's decision to fire Fedorov as part of a Cabinet reshuffle in July triggered Ukraine's largest protests during the full-scale invasion. Demonstrators took to the streets daily for more than a month all over Ukraine, with thousands protesting against Fedorov's dismissal.
Amid the protests, Fedorov emerged as a potential contender for the presidency as his approval ratings soared. After Zelensky refused to re-appoint him as defense minister earlier this month, he called for a wartime election, splitting public opinion.
“Mykhailo Fedorov has agreed to advise the Italian defense minister on modern warfare technologies in a non-staff capacity," Fedorov's press service told the Kyiv Independent. "However, his primary focus remains his work in Ukraine and projects related to the war and the development of Ukraine's defense tech sector. Mykhailo Fedorov will remain in Kyiv.”
The press service said that Fedorov and Crosetto had already met several times during Fedorov's tenure as defense minister, including during visits as part of the Ramstein format.
Fedorov said in a Facebook post that he had "begun an international trip focused on developing our new digitalization and defense tech projects."
"Our first meeting was with Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto," he added. "I thanked Guido for his personal support and for inviting me to serve as his adviser on defense innovation."
Fedorov said that, in this role, he "would help Italy develop modern warfare technologies, strengthen its defense sector, and adapt to emerging global security challenges."
He added, however, that he would "continue working in Ukraine on projects that strengthen our defense capabilities and help attract international resources."
"During the meeting, we discussed drones, autonomous systems, air defense, and the development of the defense tech ecosystem," Fedorov said.
He also said that he was continuing his international trip, "with further meetings with partners ahead to discuss digitalization, defense technology, and the development of new projects."
Fedorov's press service told the Kyiv Independent that, following his dismissal, he had received job offers from many private companies and "from partners in different fields."

articles.title: Board of Peace envoy Mladenov warns Gaza ceasefire risks ‘collapse’

Board of Peace envoy Mladenov warns Gaza ceasefire risks ‘collapse’
In an interview with Al Jazeera, Nicolay Mladenov says that a return to war would be ‘devastating’.
The failure of both sides to adhere to the roadmap for peace “threatens a collapse of the ceasefire in Gaza”, Nikolay Mladenov, the high representative for the Board of Peace, has warned in an interview with Al Jazeera.
There is “no better alternative to the current plan”, Mladenov said on Friday, adding that the “return to war would be devastating”.

His warning was “directed at both the Palestinian and Israeli sides”, he said, at a time when the besieged Strip is witnessing continued Israeli raids and attacks.
Mladenov stressed that any retreat from the commitments of the roadmap will negatively affect overall security and humanitarian arrangements in Palestine, which may return the region to a spiral of violence with dire consequences.
The Board of Peace has “determined the mechanism for deploying the International Stabilization Force [ISF] and its deployment locations in the Gaza Strip,” he said, noting that Morocco agreed to take part, though Turkiye will not participate after Israel vetoed Ankara’s involvement.
He added that the force’s “advance elements should arrive in the Gaza Strip soon”.
On reconstruction, Mladenov told Al Jazeera that the Board has received pledges worth $7bn, while crediting Qatar, Egypt and Turkiye with playing “an important role” in advancing the agreement with Hamas.
He noted talks with Israel on increasing humanitarian aid are “good”, while expressing hope that a Palestinian national committee would “assume its responsibilities in the Gaza Strip soon”.
The National Committee for the Administration of Gaza is a proposed technocratic, non-factional authority tasked with running day-to-day civil affairs. It is designed to manage public services and coordinate local reconstruction independently of Hamas and other political factions.
Where the roadmap stands
Mladenov first proposed a 15-point roadmap on May 21, covering reconstruction, disarmament of Palestinian armed groups, an Israeli gradual withdrawal, and the ISF’s mandate, alongside restructuring Gaza’s police.
The Board of Peace announced on July 31 that it had reached an agreement on the roadmap for the ceasefire’s next phase. Hamas said it had approved it and called on Israel to be held to its implementation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu subsequently rejected the plan, denying reports that his government had agreed to allow the international troops into Gaza at all. This leaves the roadmap’s status publicly contested even as the US and the Board of Peace said it’s the only viable path forward.
On the ground, Israel’s violations of the ceasefire have continued unabated. Since the ceasefire took effect in October 2025, 1,303 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli fire, and 4,336 more were wounded, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry.
The overall toll from Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023 stands at 73,438 killed and 174,447 wounded, the ministry said.
The diplomatic track
Mladenov’s warning also comes amid renewed, if uncertain, diplomatic movement.
In recent weeks, Hamas’s political chief Khalil al-Hayya held talks with Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad, before a visit to the region by US envoy Jared Kushner aimed at narrowing the gap between Israel and the Board of Peace’s plan.
The trip followed Netanyahu’s public rejection of the roadmap, with a US official saying Washington and Israel remain aligned on “the strategic goal” but that Israel has expressed “doubts” requiring further coordination.
Analysts say the roadmap’s political viability still hinges on securing genuine Israeli buy-in, which has remained unresolved despite Hamas’s stated approval and months of mediation efforts.

articles.title: CEC approves nuclear referendum, rejects other two
articles.body:
The Central Election Commission (CEC) yesterday announced it has approved holding a referendum on nuclear power, but rejected proposals on caning and traffic fines.
The Legislative Yuan on Aug. 14 approved three referendums: introducing caning as a criminal punishment, abolishing the government’s nuclear-free homeland policy and using traffic fines to improve road safety.
The commission met for more than two and a half hours, and ruled that the referendum on caning did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act (公民投票法), CEC Chairman Michael You (游盈隆) said.
Photo: Chen Yi-kuan, Taipei Times
The caning proposal, put forward by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT), seeks to introduce caning as a punishment for sexual assault, crimes against children, large-scale fraud and aggravated fraud.
However, caning or similar forms of corporal punishment are not recognized under Taiwan’s criminal justice system, You said.
The CEC therefore determined that the proposal amounted to creating new legislative principles, and was not a referendum on the initiation or repeal of a major policy, as defined by the act, he added.
The proposal involves using state power to inflict physical pain on prisoners and is considered by many countries to be cruel, inhuman and a violation of human dignity, he said.
That would contravene the Act Governing Execution of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights (公民與政治權利國際公約及經濟社會文化權利國際公約施行法), which states that no one shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment, he added.
Of the eight CEC members, seven voted that the caning proposal did not qualify as a referendum, said You, who chaired the meeting, adding that he did not cast a vote.
Regarding the Taiwan People’s Party’s (TPP) proposed referendum on earmarking traffic fines exclusively for road-related purposes, four commission members found that it did not meet the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said.
The commission held three rounds of voting, with the same 4-3 split each time, he added.
As for the proposal to repeal Taiwan’s nuclear-free homeland policy, six CEC members supported the referendum, with one abstention, You said.
The CEC ruled that the proposal meets the requirements of the Referendum Act, he said, adding that the referendum vote would be held on Nov. 28, alongside the local elections.
The KMT caucus condemned the CEC’s decision to reject the two proposals, saying that referendums exist to give people a direct say when a country faces major disputes over public policy.
“Yet what has happened now is that whether people want to vote no longer matters, and neither does whether the Legislative Yuan approves the proposal,” it said. “Instead the CEC has decided on behalf of 23 million people: ‘You are not entitled to answer this question.’”
“Is this direct democracy, or the direct confiscation of democracy?” it asked.
The TPP slammed You, saying he had claimed that “referendums submitted by the Legislative Yuan should be approved in principle and rejected only as an exception.”
“Yet he has now turned that exception into a pretext for arbitrarily expanding his powers, abandoning his principles as an academic, enabling the ruling party to flout the law and obstructing the public’s right to initiate referendums,” it said. “Such actions have brought shame on Taiwan’s democratic constitutional system.”

In the Kryvyi Rih district, an attack on the Zelenodolsk community damaged infrastructure.
Earlier on Friday, Russian forces struck Nova Poshta warehouse facilities in the Kyiv region, then hit the same site twice more in as firefighters were battling the resulting blaze.
Ukraine Hits Suspected Russian Army HQ in Apparent SCALP Strike
Around the same time, Russia also struck Zaporizhzhia’s last operating Epicentr shopping center, injuring at least four people. According to Ukrainian officials, the second drone hit approximately 30 minutes after the first, specifically targeting the emergency responders who had arrived to extinguish fires and search for survivors.
Russia continues to strike civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as emergency responders in “double-tap” attacks, violating international humanitarian law.

articles.title: Ousted Ukraine defence chief accepts job advising Italian minister
articles.body:
Ousted Ukraine defence chief accepts job advising Italian minister
KYIV - Ukraine’s ousted defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov – whose sacking in July prompted rare wartime protests – on Aug 28 said he had accepted a job working as an advisor to Italy’s defence minister.
Fedorov, a tech-savvy 35-year-old, was dismissed as defence minister in July after reports of ructions between him and the country’s military leadership.
His sacking by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky prompted thousands to protest across Ukraine, many of whom called for him to be reinstated to the role.
Fedorov said on Aug 28 he had agreed to become “advisor on defence innovation” to Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto, six weeks after his dismissal.
“In this role, I will help Italy develop technologies for modern warfare, improve its defence sector, and adapt to the world’s new security challenges,” Fedorov said.
Crosetto told Italy’s La Repubblica newspaper in July that he had offered Fedorov the job.
Fedorov will continue living and working in Kyiv for the role, his press office said.
There was no immediate comment from the Ukrainian presidential administration.
The Italian defence ministry in a statement said the announcement was “an important opportunity” for Italy and said he would serve as “Innovation Advisor”.
The statement said Italy welcomed “engagement with partners who have gained significant experience in the field, especially in autonomous systems and air defence”.
Fedorov had been a longtime Zelensky ally, having worked with the president since he took office in 2019.
Relations between the two soured after his sacking, with Fedorov earlier in August calling for Ukraine to hold elections that had been postponed since Russia invaded in 2022.
Zelensky rejected the proposal as risky and divisive. AFP

articles.title: Ceuta warns it is 'on the brink of collapse' as Spain seeks Frontex and Europol help
articles.body:
Meanwhile, Spain's interior minister called for calm after Ceuta residents clashed with police during protests against migrants who have remained in the enclave following a mass influx.
Spain has asked the European Commission (EC) for the support from Frontex and Europol to assist with the screening of migrants who are staying irregularly in Ceuta, according to several Spanish media outlets.
Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska has asked the EC for Frontex, Europol and the European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA) to "reinforce the device set up to address the management of the triage and subsequent processing of the personal files of the immigrants who still remain in Ceuta irregularly."
The Interior Ministry also demanded the extension of Operation Minerva, a joint initiative of the Spanish police and the EU border protection agency Frontex.
Madrid ask that that operation run until 2 September until "the situation created in the autonomous city is resolved."
Madrid also asked for the " assistance of the European Union Agency for Asylum in conducting interviews and providing interpreters" in order to triage migrants.
Due to space limitations in Ceuta, this process is expected to be carried out electronically.
The Interior Ministry announced on Friday that Ceuta's border would be reinforced with a package of "extraordinary" measures such as extending the Tarajal and Benzú breakwaters, a permanent system of maritime containment buoys, aerial surveillance with drones, light intervention vessels and remotely operated underwater devices.
At the same time, Ceuta's Assembly unanimously called on the central government on Friday to act "immediately and without further delay" arguing that the city is in an "extreme situation, on the verge of collapse."
The Board of Spokespersons, together with the non-affiliated MPs, unanimously approved on Friday an institutional declaration calling on the government to adopt urgent measures one month after the mass entry of at least 72,000 migrants from Morocco.
"Ceuta has lost its way of life and its calm. We do not have much time to avert disaster," Ceuta's President Juan Vivas warned.
The declaration calls for a return to their countries, "in accordance with the law" of those who took part in the mass entry and are still in Ceuta. It also backs citizens' right to demonstrate, as long as it is done "peacefully and in an orderly manner," and condemns violent incidents recorded in recent days.
"No one can or should take the law into their own hands. The defence of Ceuta and the interests of its people can only be pursued through legality," Vivas said.
Appeal for calm
Meanwhile, Spain's interior minister called for calm on Friday after residents of Ceuta clashed with police during protests against migrants who have remained in the North African enclave following a mass influx.
Tensions have been high in the territory of 80,000 people since at least 72,000 people crossed into Ceuta over several days in July, triggering a Europe-wide migrant alert.
Spain's leftist government says most have since left the enclave of 18.5 square kilometres but thousands remain wandering the streets and sleeping on beaches.
Demonstrations have intensified in recent days, with some protesters clashing with police on Thursday at a beach where migrants have been sleeping. Some of their belongings were burned.
A soldier was injured in a separate incident on Thursday when migrants threw stones at troops, while 12 Moroccan migrants were arrested.
Two more arrests were made after migrants attacked a police officer, sources said.
"Violence is not the answer," Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told parliament on Friday.
"I call for calm and an end to any form of violence, because...violence is not the way to resolve any problem with the complexity" of that facing Ceuta, he added.
Right-wing and far-right parties have demanded that all the migrants be rounded up and sent back to their home countries.
Grande-Marlaska accused them of "inciting hatred and confrontation" in Ceuta.
The government has warned that each individual must be identified to determine whether they are entitled to asylum or subject to deportation, while unaccompanied migrant children require special protection.
Ceuta and Melilla, another small Spanish territory in North Africa, form Europe's only land border with Africa.

articles.title: Key Zelensky staff arrested over money laundering to bailout ex-minister
articles.body:
Key Zelensky staff arrested over money laundering to bailout ex-minister
Ukraine’s central bank has launched an anti-money laundering probe into several lenders who processed a bail payment for former Justice and Energy Minister German Galushchenko, amid fresh allegations of high-level corruption in Kiev.
Earlier this month, Western-backed anti-corruption agencies accused a group of officials, including a deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky’s office, of laundering about $3.3 million in cash to secure Galushchenko’s release on bail.
Galushchenko, who was arrested and charged with money laundering and membership of a criminal organization after attempting to leave Ukraine, is also a suspect in a separate corruption case linked to Timur Mindich, self-exiled in Israel but known widely as ‘Zelensky’s bagman’.
Ukrainian state-owned Sense Bank temporarily disabled fraud detection systems at the same time that some $1.7 million in cash – intended for Galushchenko’s bail – was allegedly laundered and processed, records released by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO) indicate.
Sense Bank is the former Ukrainian branch of Alfa Bank, which Kiev nationalized in 2023 under the guise of enforcing sanctions on Russia.
Ukraine’s central bank said Thursday that it is also investigating several other institutions linked to the bail payments.
Mindich’s man in the government
Galushchenko was arrested in February and charged with large-scale money laundering in connection with an alleged criminal network operated by Mindich, who himself fled Ukraine to Israel after NABU accused him of extorting $100 million in kickbacks from state atomic energy company Energoatom.
Galushchenko was duly released on $3.3 million bail in late June, upon receipt of cash by the authorities reportedly from four dubious sources.
NABU surveillance audio files suggest that Zelensky’s deputy head of office, Irina Mudraya, and others, used influence at Sense Bank to convert bags of cash into bank transfers to the account of the High Anti-Corruption Court. Investigators filmed the cash being delivered, according to the case materials. Mudraya, who is accused of administering the scheme, was subsequently arrested and fired.
Who controls Sense Bank?
Recordings linked to Mindich previously leaked to the media include a discussion between one of his associates and a former adviser to the bank’s CEO about impending changes to its supervisory council, and during which the body’s current head, Nikolay Gladyshenko, was identified as a suitable candidate.
Gladyshenko and the bank’s current head, Aleksey Stupak, allegedly approved the bail payment scheme. Sense Bank’s director of financial monitoring, Lyudmila Snigur, who has since been suspended, was reportedly threatened with dismissal unless her department skipped human reviews of transactions made during “maintenance” of the automated systems.
Control relinquished by ‘Israeli refugee Timur’
The Mudraya case materials depict Sense Bank as being in a vulnerable position and seeking new protection with the permission of “Israeli refugee Timur” – presumably Mindich. This allegedly made the bank susceptible to “requests” to launder money for Galushchenko.
“People from Sense Bank today were like a balm to a wound,” Mudraya allegedly said after bank executives met officials from Zelensky’s office. “They crawled to us like kittens: ‘Please, please, take us!’”
Doubts about Ukraine’s anti-laundering system
NABU’s allegations have further embarrassed the central bank as its reputation disintegrates in the fallout from the corruption surrounding Zelensky. The regulator launched an investigation into Gladyshenko in May after his possible links to Mindich became public, but maintains that it did not have enough evidence before the latest revelations to declare him unsuitable for the position.
Gladyshenko announced he was recusing himself from his role, but this “did not exclude his actual influence on the bank’s operations,” the central bank conceded last week.
The central bank insists the Mudraya case demonstrates that its anti-money-laundering system is effective, but has confirmed that it is also investigating other banks that may also have participated in the cash-to-bail scheme run out of Vladimir Zelensky’s office.

articles.title: New Report: Space Force Spent $124M on Commercial Data, Services over Nearly 3 Years
articles.body:
The Space Force spent nearly $124 million on commercial space data and services between 2023 and 2025—and a little known interagency working group could help facilitate even more data buys going forward.
A new Government Accountability Office report tracked Space Force, National Reconnaissance Office, and National Geospatial Intelligence Agency purchases of space data and services from private sector firms between January 2023 and September 2025. This includes things like imagery and electro-optical observations as well as analytic reports and services that allow the agencies to identify potential positioning, navigation, and timing interference.
The Space Force uses a contractor-run platform called the Global Data Marketplace to buy much of its commercial data. GAO found that the Joint Commercial Operations cell— a U.S. Space Command-managed organization—was the largest purchaser during the time frame it tracked, accounting for about 62 percent of its spending, or $76 million.
System Delta 810, which delivers space-based sensing and targeting capabilities, bought about $35 million through the marketplace during that time frame, and other Pentagon organizations purchased around $4.6 million.
Because NRO and NGA budgets are classified, GAO couldn’t provide detailed spending information. However, it found that the NRO spent an average of between $300 million and $500 million annually during those years, and the NGA an average of between $25 million and $125 million—specifically for commercial analytic products like aeronautical, maritime, and topographical imagery.
Congress directed the report in the Fiscal 2023 National Defense Authorization Act amid concerns that the Defense Department wasn’t investing enough in commercial data and services. While all three organizations have emphasized a need to better leverage commercial capabilities, lawmakers have pushed for more investment. In fact, the House Armed Services Committee’s version of the fiscal ‘27 defense policy bill included several provisions calling on the Space Force to integrate more commercial data and transition more demonstrations into operational programs.
The White House has also emphasized the need to buy more commercial products instead of bespoke military solutions, issuing a December 2025 executive order that identified commercial integration as key to building a resilient space architecture.
Of note, GAO’s report focused specifically on commercial data and analytic services, which doesn’t encompass the full range of commercial technology or systems that the Space Force may leverage. The service has said its fiscal ‘27 budget request includes more than $2.5 billion in commercial capabilities and services across a number of programs.
One potential barrier to the Space Force better incorporating commercially available data is a lack of understanding within some organizations about how to purchase it and the regulations that govern its use. GAO found that, for example, some Space Force offices were unaware they could access licensed data that was purchased by the Joint Commercial Operations cell and others had concerns about data availability and cost.
“These challenges led to hesitation to purchase and use commercial data among some potential users,” GAO said.
The watchdog report found that a little-known organization called the Cross-Government Commercial Data Sharing Working Group, composed of various DOD offices and other federal agencies, meets regularly to discuss options for data sharing, address issues and concerns from user groups, and even to coordinate data buys. However, GAO said, many of the offices that could benefit from this group were unaware it exists.
“While the working group operates regularly and has increased collaboration among agencies that already purchase commercial space data, some Space Force officials were not aware of its existence,” the report stated. “We reviewed Space Force public websites, publicly accessible JCO presentations, and Intelink, an internal government website, for information about the informal working group and did not find this information.”
The Space Force acknowledged the need for better visibility and concurred with a GAO recommendation that it raise awareness about the group.

articles.title: Iran says still open to diplomacy as war with US hits six months
articles.body:
Iran says still open to diplomacy as war with US hits six months
TEHRAN - Iran left the door open to diplomacy on Aug 28, six months into a war with the United States that has upended the Middle East, but only if Washington abandons its pressure campaign.
“Putting diplomacy back on track isn’t impossible. It hinges on US understanding of one simple fact: pressure doesn’t work,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X on Aug 28.
Diplomatic efforts, spearheaded by mediators including Pakistan and Qatar, have tried for months to bring an end to the war started by the US and Israel in late February to no avail.
While a ceasefire was agreed in April and a memorandum of understanding towards a final peace deal was signed in June, no agreement has been forthcoming and Washington has since declared “economic warfare” against Tehran.
In the latest effort to reinvigorate diplomacy, Araghchi met his Qatari counterpart on Aug 27 in the Iranian capital to discuss the Strait of Hormuz, closed by the Islamic republic at the start of the war, at the tail end of a week of intense Iranian talks with Oman and Pakistan.
A US naval counterblockade of Iranian ports is squeezing petrol supplies in Iran, amid a shortfall of domestic production, as the US ramps up pressure on its foe, declaring an “economic D-Day”.
The April ceasefire put an end to the most intense fighting, but sporadic attacks, mainly around the Strait of Hormuz, have dimmed the prospects of a final peace agreement.
In a statement on Aug 28, US Senator Jack Reed criticised President Donald Trump over the war.
“Six months later, not a single objective has been achieved,” said Reed, the top Democrat on the Senate Armed Services Committee.
“Indeed, he has weakened our position in the Middle East and the world significantly.”
‘Build trust’
Tehran has for weeks been holding talks on the future of Hormuz with Muscat, whose territorial waters account for the other half of the strait, while insisting that Hormuz will remain closed so long as Washington has not fulfilled its commitments under the June memorandum, which calls for lifting the US counterblockade and removing sanctions.
“The US should build trust, speak respectfully, acknowledge our rights and uphold commitments,” Araghchi said.
Iranian lawmaker Esmail Kowsari reiterated to state television on Aug 28 that if the memorandum was not implemented and the US “does not respect its commitments, not only will the Strait of Hormuz remain closed, but the United States must be ready for our offensive actions and we will seek them in the most distant places”.
While Washington now aims to crush Iran economically, Tehran has weathered decades of international sanctions and experts remain sceptical about how much more pressure the US can bring to bear.
Analysts say the US plan to isolate Iran would require unlikely cooperation from trading partner China, which has defended its cooperation with Tehran and vowed to safeguard its interests.
China remains able to buy Iranian crude, an important source of revenue for Tehran, via overland routes not reliant on the Strait of Hormuz.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said “no one is above the reach of US sanctions” when asked if Washington would target Chinese banks that do business with Iran, ahead of an expected September visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping to the US capital. AFP

articles.title: Navy wargamed hybrid fleet and still needs crewed warships
articles.body:
The Royal Navy has run a series of service-wide war games to test its planned hybrid fleet, and the answer has come back consistently that crewed warships remain necessary alongside the uncrewed systems, the First Sea Lord has said, in an interview for the Council on Geostrategy’s Defence Talks podcast.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins, the first Royal Marine to lead the service, was asked whether the ease with which a surface ship can now be found and attacked calls into question the purpose of having one at all.
He said the transition does not make crewed warships irrelevant, but changes how they are used. “It just changes the way that you’re going to operate them, and it changes the way you achieve mass. It changes what their role is, in particular the command and control and coordination of the uncrewed systems that we’re going to need to field.”
On the testing itself, he said: “That’s why we have been running a series of navy-wide war games to test the hybrid fleet and rigorously test it in each environment as to how we’re going to operate and how this would work, where the challenges and the weaknesses are in the model at the moment. Time and again, the tests come back with you still need conventional warships in this mix. They’re just further back and have a slightly different role to the way that we would have fielded them in the past.”
That is a more reassuring answer than much of the surrounding debate has assumed, and it is being reached through structured testing rather than asserted. The Navy is examining where its own model breaks before committing to it, which is a considerably better position than discovering the weaknesses later.
General Jenkins also pushed back on reading the Black Sea across to British waters wholesale. “We do have to be careful applying the geography and the specific physical environment of the Black Sea or the Straits of Hormuz to some of our Atlantic space, and the big Atlantic is a very different proposition to some of those quite constrained and even reasonably benign waters.” He immediately added that this implies no complacency.
What Ukraine has achieved he described as a wake-up call for every Western navy, noting that a navy in name but not in being had neutralised one of the most advanced fleets in the world.
He set the change alongside earlier turning points in naval history, from sail to steam and wood to iron, through the dreadnought, the aircraft carrier and the submarine, observing that each had its detractors at the time, and that those arguing steam would never replace sail or that carriers were irrelevant were eventually answered by events.
Listen to the full interview
The conversation runs a good deal wider than the extracts covered here. Over the course of the episode the First Sea Lord also discusses reforming officer selection and training, how the Navy intends to unleash innovation at the front line, the three strands of the Atlantic programme in Bastion, Strike and Shield, the relationship with industry that the hybrid fleet depends on, and his own reading of how the strategic picture has changed since he joined the military at the end of the Cold War. Interviews with a serving First Sea Lord at this length are rare, and anyone with an interest in where the Royal Navy is heading over the next decade will get considerably more from listening to it in full than from any write-up.
General Sir Gwyn Jenkins was interviewed by Viktorija Starych-Samueliene and Paul Mason. The episode is available on YouTube, Spotify and Apple Podcasts.
Defence Talks is produced by the Council on Geostrategy, a London-based think tank founded in 2021 which focuses on British foreign, defence and trade policy, the Indo-Pacific and the geopolitics of technology, and which publishes the journal Britain’s World alongside its research output. The series is delivered in partnership with ADS Group, the trade association representing the British aerospace, defence, security and space industries, and is sponsored by BAE Systems.

articles.title: SK Hynix starts construction at site in US’ Indiana
articles.body:
SK Hynix Inc on Thursday held a groundbreaking ceremony for its advanced memory packaging facility in Indiana, marking a milestone in Washington’s expansive campaign to rebuild domestic supply chains and manufacturing for strategically important sectors.
The West Lafayette plant, costing more than US$4 billion and occupying a 54-hectare site, is to be SK Hynix’s first high-bandwidth memory (HBM) packaging base in the US. Its cleanroom is expected to open by October 2028, with mass production of next-generation HBM scheduled to begin in the second half of 2029, chief executive officer Kwak Noh-jung said at the event.
When fully operational, it would be a major HBM hub employing about 1,000 people, Kwak said.
Photo: Reuters
HBM is an indispensable part of the global artificial intelligence (AI) hardware boom, as it is prerequisite for assembling Nvidia Corp’s most advanced AI acceleration systems.
That has helped SK Hynix grow to become South Korea’s second-most valuable company, behind Samsung Electronics Co, which has also been lifted by runaway demand for HBM and other memory products.
The Indiana project is backed by the US CHIPS and Science Act, a signature law signed by then-US president Joe Biden in 2022 that allowed for the South Korean chipmaker to receive as much as US$458 million in direct funding and up to US$500 million in loans.
The program was designed to reduce US dependence on overseas semiconductor production and bring critical chip manufacturing, packaging and research capabilities to US soil.
At the event, Kwak said the plant would help strengthen a domestic AI chip supply chain in the US that Washington views as essential to economic and national security.
“We will expand our investments and collaboration in the US, grow together and become the most trusted partner in shaping the future of AI in America,” he said.
The Indiana investment is particularly significant because it targets a weak link in the US semiconductor supply chain: advanced packaging.
The technology combines multiple chips into a single package, often stacking them vertically to boost performance, as conventional tech miniaturization approaches become increasingly difficult.
Wafers produced by SK Hynix in South Korea would be shipped to Indiana for packaging and testing before being supplied to US customers, the company said.
The project is expected to create about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs through construction, operations and related industries.
SK Hynix is considering more than 100 companies to supply materials, components and equipment, potentially creating a broader semiconductor cluster.
SK Hynix also signed an agreement with nearby Purdue University to cooperate on HBM, system integration and advanced packaging research.
An advanced packaging research and development test bed would be built alongside the production lines.
Reflecting Indiana’s historic ties with South Korea — the state sent about 140,000 troops to the Korean War — parent SK Group also said it would provide new employment and career opportunities for former US Forces Korea service members.

articles.title: Population to plummet, council warns
articles.body:
Taiwan’s population is projected to shrink by almost half over the next five decades, intensifying labor shortages and placing a growing drag on economic growth as the technology-intensive economy confronts a rapidly aging workforce.
The population is expected to fall to 12.15 million by 2075, a 48 percent decline from this year, National Development Council projections released yesterday showed.
The decline would fundamentally alter Taiwan’s workforce. From 2037, more than half of the working-age population is projected to be aged between 45 and 64, signaling the end of an era when the economy could rely on a relatively large labor force.
Photo: CNA
The shift threatens to challenge Taiwan’s growth model, which depends on a broad manufacturing workforce and a growing supply of highly skilled workers to support its semiconductor and artificial intelligence industries.
A shrinking pool of workers could make recruitment increasingly difficult, while a growing elderly population would add pressure on social spending and public finances.
The projections also point to a deeper demographic problem — Taiwan is not only losing its population, but failing to replenish it, the council said.
It lowered its long-term fertility assumptions after the fertility rate fell to a record low 0.695 last year, significantly below previous estimates.
The number of women aged 20 to 49 has declined since peaking in 2005, while the proportion of married women in that age group has also fallen.
The shrinking pool of potential mothers is making a sustained recovery in births increasingly difficult, it said.
Taiwan’s population is projected to fall below 20 million in 2045, dropping to 19.98 million.
People aged 65 or older are expected to account for 37 percent of the population, while the working-age population would shrink to 57.9 percent and children to just 5.2 percent, the council said.
By 2075, the imbalance would be even more pronounced, with older people projected to comprise 52.9 percent of the population, working-age people 42.3 percent and children 4.8 percent, it said.
The dependency ratio — the number of children and elderly people relative to those of working age — is projected to rise from 55.2 dependents for every 100 working-age people to 136.6 by 2075, the council said.
The potential support ratio is expected to fall below one, suggesting less than one working-age person for every person aged 65 or older, it said.
The government is preparing the economy for a permanently smaller workforce. It has established a population strategy task force, and in May launched 18 measures covering childbirth support, childcare, education, workplace policies and housing.
Additional policy packages would target elderly people, talent development across all age groups and the recruitment of overseas talent, the council said.
For businesses, the implications extend beyond hiring. Companies are likely to face greater pressure to raise labor force participation among elderly people, attract workers from overseas, and accelerate automation and productivity gains.

articles.title: DPP China Affairs warns of election interference
articles.body:
With Taiwan’s year-end local elections approaching, the Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) China Affairs Department has warned that cooperating with Chinese election interference could carry a sentence of up to 15 years in prison, while those who report foreign interference could receive rewards of up to NT$20 million (US$632,351).
The department outlined seven types of illegal conduct involving Chinese election interference.
One form of interference is recruiting tour groups at China’s direction. That means accepting Chinese instructions, commissions or funding to recruit borough chiefs, local figures or voters to participate in a tour including transportation, accommodation or meals and asking them to support specific political parties or candidates, the department said.
Photo: Chen Cheng-yu, Taipei Times
Another form of election interference is recruiting people for free or significantly underpriced tours in exchange for votes, which could constitute bribery even without directly receiving instructions from China, it said.
Accepting any travel, accommodation or other benefits in exchange for political support could also be illegal if the person knowingly agrees to vote for a specific political party or candidate, the office said.
Producing or publishing fake opinion polls using foreign funding or at China’s direction to manipulate elections, influence voters or shape cooperation between political parties could constitute election interference, it said.
Assisting China with propaganda by accepting its instructions, commissions or funding to campaign for specific candidates, speak at rallies, hold press conferences, produce promotional materials or conduct media campaigns is also election interference, it said.
Serving as an intermediary to relay instructions related to election interference, such as helping China find, direct or fund people in Taiwan to mobilize supporters, promote candidates or conduct online operations, could also result in penalties, it added.
Lastly, developing organizations or gathering intelligence for China, as well as spying on, collecting or handing over official secrets, could constitute more serious national security offenses, it said.
These seven types of conduct could contravene the Anti-Infiltration Act (反滲透法), the National Security Act (國家安全法), the Election and Recall Act (公職人員選舉罷免法), the Presidential and Vice Presidential Election and Recall Act (總統副總統選罷法) or the Criminal Code, with penalties of up to 15 years in prison, the department said.
Criminal liability could extend beyond those who accept money to people who recruit others, relay instructions, mobilize supporters, spread propaganda or accept benefits to vote for a particular candidate, it said.
People who encounter suspected election interference should hold onto evidence such as messages, itineraries, payment records, photos and videos, and call 0800-024-099 and press 4 to report them to prosecutors or investigators, it said.
It urged people not to accept benefits, travel to China, follow Chinese instructions nor assist with propaganda to protect democracy, freedom and Taiwan’s right to determine its own future.

articles.title: Groups press Merz over China policy
articles.body:
German industry is increasing pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz to take a tougher line with Beijing, with companies calling for greater action to address what they describe as unfair competition from Chinese rivals.
The growing assertiveness from German business representatives marks a shift in a country that long resisted trade barriers for fear of Chinese retaliation. How Berlin positions itself will help shape the EU’s broader trade stance toward China, with talks between the bloc and Beijing scheduled for October.
An Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) report published in June said that Chinese manufacturers received three to eight times more state support than OECD rivals relative to revenue, with subsidies accounting for nearly 60 percent of their global market-share gains.
Photo: AFP
Germany’s trade deficit with its biggest trading partner widened by about 22 billion euros (US$25.6 billion) last year to 89.3 billion euros as imports into the European country rose 8.8 percent and exports fell 9.7 percent.
“We need to discuss with China what is happening. If it is confirmed that this is attributable to subsidies or unfair competition, then it is an issue,” said Volker Treier, head of foreign trade at the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
The concern is particularly pressing for German automakers such as Volkswagen, which — having been overtaken by local brands such as BYD Co (比亞迪) in China — now face growing competition from Chinese rivals in the European market.
Merz’s coalition has sharpened its language on China, but its messages remain mixed, combining calls to reduce economic dependencies with an insistence that the country remains an important economic partner.
Following signs of division on the matter within his coalition, Merz said on Wednesday that he had asked the Cabinet to work on proposals to address trade imbalances between the EU and China.
“We note that German industry, too, has apparently changed its mind regarding these global imbalances,” the chancellor said, pointing to associations such as the VDA representing automakers, which is reconsidering its previous opposition to protective measures.
Siemens Energy chief executive officer Christian Bruch in June said that treating Chinese imports like European products was “not acceptable,” adding that regulations needed to be put in place and local content quotas considered.
Treier said there were sufficient instruments in the WTO and the EU framework to defend European industry.
“We simply need to streamline and shorten our decisionmaking processes when we decide to act,” he said.
The BDI, representing major German manufacturers, is advocating for the faster application of trade policy instruments, including safeguards and methodological adjustments, such as bundling product groups in anti-dumping and anti-subsidy proceedings.
“The situation is intensifying due to the massive price pressure we face from Chinese suppliers,” BDI executive board member Wolfgang Niedermark said.
“Possible countermeasures by China must be included in strategic considerations, but should not determine or ultimately prevent Europe’s actions,” Niedermark added.
