“Retailers and suppliers are rebuilding logistics, relocating stocks, changing routes and storage formats. It is more complicated, takes longer and costs more, but the system is adapting. There is currently no threat of a systemic physical shortage of basic food products,” Vysotskyi said.
He acknowledged that consumers could see changes in product ranges or temporary shortages of individual goods at particular stores, but stressed that the country’s overall food supply remains secure.
At the same time, the destruction of warehouses has raised questions over how losses from products destroyed in Russian attacks should be covered. Vysotskyi noted that the supply and sale of goods are governed by commercial and contractual relationships between producers, distributors, and retail chains.
The minister said the risks should be shared fairly among all parties involved rather than falling entirely on one participant in the supply chain.
“A fair approach would be to distribute risks proportionally among all parties. This does not necessarily mean 50-50. Different products have different margins, terms of cooperation and economic results. Therefore, the mechanism should be determined separately for each product category and take into account how profits are distributed between the parties,” Vysotskyi said.
A similar approach should apply to the additional costs associated with restructuring logistics networks, which businesses are currently adapting in real time, according to the minister.
The comments come after a large-scale Russian overnight attack struck logistics infrastructure in the Kyiv region, damaging or destroying distribution facilities used by several of Ukraine’s leading retail and consumer companies.
Among the businesses affected were Fora, Budynok Ihrashok, Comfy, Epicentr, Aurora, Silpo, and Roshen, Forbes Ukraine reported on August 27, citing statements from company executives.

articles.title: "Black-market transplant specialists" in Bukovyna set up a scheme to sell anatomical materials from the deceased; suspects detained — Prosecutor General
articles.body:
"Black-market transplant specialists" in Bukovyna set up a scheme to sell anatomical materials from the deceased; suspects detained — Prosecutor General
Kyiv • UNN
Four employees of a pathological anatomy bureau are suspected of illegally removing and selling tissue from deceased individuals. They have been detained.
Law enforcement officers uncovered a scheme involving the illegal trade in the organs and tissues of deceased people in Bukovyna. The criminal activity was organized by officials of the Chernivtsi Regional Pathology Bureau. As Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko reported, four employees of the pathology bureau were notified of suspicion, reports UNN.
Details
According to the Prosecutor General, each participant in the "scheme" had a specific role — from interacting with the relatives of the deceased and preparing fictitious documents to the direct removal of anatomical materials and their subsequent transportation to customers.
Skin, bones, tendons, corneas and other tissues were removed from the bodies of the deceased. They were sold to companies that manufacture bioimplants for surgery and dentistry. The bureau did not have a license to practice transplant medicine, so trade with recipient companies was concealed by fictitious agreements on "scientific and medical cooperation," while the transfer of tissues was documented as the "supply of raw materials for the manufacture of bioimplants." With some clients, they worked without contractual relations
According to the Prosecutor General, relatives of the deceased were manipulatively persuaded to consent to such procedures by being offered free embalming or body storage, as well as discounts on other services. At the same time, people were unaware of the actual extent of the removals and the subsequent sale of the tissues.
Cases were also documented in which relatives of the deceased refused to give consent, but anatomical materials were removed against their will. In another episode, consent was obtained from an employee of a geriatric nursing home who cared for the deceased person, although the burial was handled by relatives, who were not asked anything.
The collected materials were delivered to recipients by rail in containers with refrigerant. In particular, the transfer of ten boxes of biomaterials was documented, as well as the shipment of corneas by the Chernivtsi–Odesa train. Official payment for such "services" was transferred to the bureau's account under acceptance-and-transfer certificates for services provided. At the same time, every month the scheme's participants received "shadow cash" through currency exchange offices, which they divided among themselves depending on their roles and the number of removals
Currently, four employees of the Chernivtsi Regional Pathology Bureau have been detained. They were notified of suspicion of illegally trading in human anatomical materials, committed by a group of persons acting in prior conspiracy (Part 5 of Article 143 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine). Searches were conducted at the bureau's premises, as well as at the suspects' residences and in their vehicles.
A human body is not a commodity, and a family's grief is not an opportunity to make money. Everyone who turned medical activity into a "black market" will receive an appropriate legal assessment. The investigation is ongoing. We will continue working

articles.title: Iran says it agreed with Oman on Hormuz passage route, links reopening to US commitments
articles.body:
Rania Abushamala
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Friday that Tehran had agreed with Oman on a passage route through the Strait of Hormuz and would reopen the strategic waterway if the US fulfilled its commitments under the Islamabad Memorandum signed in June.
“We agreed with Oman on the passage route through Hormuz, and if the US fulfills its commitments under the memorandum of understanding, we will open the strait,” Pezeshkian said, according to Iranian official news agency IRNA.
Pezeshkian said the passage route had also been communicated to Iran’s supreme leader.
“We are now following up on the matter. If the US fulfills its commitments regarding lifting the sanctions and blockade, releasing assets, beginning investment and ending the war in Lebanon, we will also open the Strait of Hormuz,” he said.
“As far as the talks have progressed, they also accept that we must return to the memorandum of understanding,” he added, referring to the US side.
Pezeshkian said Iran’s Supreme National Security Council had reached what he called an “exceptional” consensus on the agreement, with 12 of its 13 members voting in favor.
“This collective wisdom was a major achievement,” he said.
The Iranian president said sanctions and the blockade were initially lifted, while negotiations began on releasing frozen Iranian funds and plans were being prepared for $300 billion in investment.
Iran, for its part, was working to restore the Strait of Hormuz to its previous status, he added. “But because they did not comply, the memorandum of understanding collapsed.”
Iran and Oman have been holding talks on an arrangement to manage shipping through the waterway since the memorandum agreed between Washington and Tehran collapsed last month.
Under that deal, the US and Iran agreed to extend an April ceasefire and gradually allow shipping through the strait to return to its prewar levels while they held talks on a final settlement to end the war that began in February.

articles.title: Large fire near Wembley Stadium disrupts tube and rail services
articles.body:
A large fire has broken out at a waste facility close to Wembley Stadium in north-west London, disrupting tube and train lines in the area.
Twenty fire engines and about 125 firefighters were sent to tackle the blaze at a mixed-waste facility on an industrial estate in Neasden, just under a mile from the venue.
Huge plumes of smoke could be seen in videos posted on social media, and more than 70 calls were made about the blaze.
There was no service on the entire Metropolitan line, which runs close to the blaze, and no service between Wembley Park and West Hampstead on the Jubilee line, with severe delays on the rest of the line, Transport for London said.
Rail services into London Marylebone were also disrupted.
A nearby Amazon warehouse, which is not related to the industrial unit involved, has been evacuated, according to PA Media.
The London fire brigade said: “Tube services on the Metropolitan and Jubilee lines will be impacted as crews respond. Rail services into London Marylebone are also disrupted as a result of this fire.”
The cause of the fire is not yet known.
It is the third major fire at a recycling centre in London this summer after two incidents at the Landmann Way Reuse and Recycling Centre in south-east London.
Fires at recycling centres caused by wrongly discarded lithium batteries, such as those found in vapes, are occurring at the rate of more than 10 a week, according to figures from the Environmental Services Association.
Battery fires at waste facilities are estimated to cost £1bn a year and are causing growing frustration among fire chiefs.

The institution, which will train civilian and military recruits, will be modelled on the famous military school at West Point
US President Donald Trump on Friday announced the creation of a “Space Academy” to train future civilian and military recruits for an arena where the United States faces rivalry with China.
Speaking at Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre in Houston, Trump said the institution would be modelled on the famed US military academy at West Point.
“It’s called the US Space Academy. That’s a big deal,” Trump said as he signed an executive order creating the new school.
“It’ll serve both the United States Space Force as well as Nasa and the civilian space flight industry, and it’ll attract, train, and graduate the very best of our nation.”
Trump has credited the US Space Force, the sixth branch of the US armed forces, with an important role in the recent American military operations in Venezuela and Iran.
He did not say where the new academy would be built.

articles.title: Mexico’s disappearances crisis could affect 165,000 children: Report
articles.body:
Maryam Ashalem de Andres
28 August 2026•Update: 28 August 2026
Around 165,000 children and adolescents in Mexico could have a missing parent, according to an exploratory estimate by human rights organization Tejiendo Redes Infancia, local media reported Friday.
The organization published a report titled “Daughters and Sons of Missing Persons in Mexico,” highlighting the impact of disappearances on children who remain largely invisible in official records.
Juan Martin Perez Garcia, regional coordinator of Tejiendo Redes Infancia, said the estimate was not an exact count but was intended to highlight gaps in official data on the family ties of missing people and how those gaps affect public policies for indirect victims.
The estimate is based on 103,176 people aged 15 to 49 who were registered as missing or not located in Mexico as of August 2026, according to the report.
Tejiendo Redes Infancia applied a national average of 1.60 children per person, based on Mexico’s 2023 National Survey of Population Dynamics, to estimate that 165,081 children could potentially be affected by the disappearances, local media reported.
Mexico’s National Registry of Missing and Not Located Persons (RNPDNO) records missing people but does not identify their children, their ages, who cares for them or what support they receive.
The organization said the lack of such information prevents authorities from identifying these children as indirect victims and from designing policies and allocating resources to protect and assist them.
The report said the disappearance of a parent can disrupt childcare, reduce household income, affect children’s education and increase insecurity, stigma and the risk of revictimization.
Tejiendo Redes Infancia called on Mexican authorities to create a specific mechanism to identify, protect and assist children whose parents have disappeared.
Perez Garcia also called for dedicated public funding, saying there is currently no specific budget to address the needs of these children.
The organization said the absence of family information also places a greater burden of care on mothers, grandmothers, siblings, partners and other relatives.
The report comes as Mexico continues to face a major crisis of missing and disappeared people, with more than 100,000 cases involving people aged 15 to 49 alone, according to the organization’s analysis.

articles.title: ‘I want Adam Levine to bring me the cake’: Israeli pop star Nunu on five years of war and music
articles.body:
On a sweltering Tuesday night at the Barby, Israeli pop star Nunu was handed a birthday cake on stage by comedian Guri Alfi, flanked by guest stars Static and Guy Mazig. The crowd was screaming, the show was entirely sold out, and, for a fleeting moment, it felt like the dizzying, untroubled heights of 2022 all over again.
It was a celebration of five years in the spotlight, but the triumph under the stage lights masked a much grittier reality. For Neomi Aharoni-Gal – the 27-year-old mastermind behind the hyper-stylized Nunu persona – reaching this milestone wasn’t just about churning out hits; it was a masterclass in creative survival.
Between stadium-sized euphoria and the sudden, crushing silence of wartime, Nunu’s five-year trajectory offers a raw look at what it actually takes to sustain an artistic vision in a market prone to fracturing overnight.
Nunu's journey from stadium highs to backstage ecstasy
Every pop career relies on a catalyst, and for Nunu, it arrived in 2022 when she was booked to open for Maroon 5 at Yarkon Park. It was a trial by fire: thrusting a fresh, avant-garde club act onto a massive stadium stage.
“I think one of the most fun moments I’ve had, maybe the most fun day of my life, was opening for Maroon 5,” Nunu recalls. “That was one of my very first shows with my band, playing songs we had never performed live on such a massive stage before. We were all completely in the clouds – up in the clouds. I remember us coming off the stage and just jamming in a total state of ecstasy because the high was so intense.”
While headliner Adam Levine operated in strict, high-security isolation – “he arrives in a car, goes straight to the stage, and gets right back into the car afterward,” she notes – just being there was an unforgettable rush. “It doesn’t matter. Just to see him and simply be there... there are no words.”
The price of silence: Shelving ‘Haganuz’
The true test of that resilience came on October 7, 2023. As geopolitical conflict halted the nation, the local music industry dissolved overnight. For an artist, the financial and emotional toll of a sudden national crisis is brutal, but for Nunu, it meant making the painful decision to completely shelve a finished studio album.
“Of course, there was the human difficulty and the massive reality check of October 7,” Nunu opens up. “It was an immense pain in its own right, just in daily life – living through a war here is a heavy weight, and compared to that, everything else shrinks into comparison. But professionally, one of the hardest and most painful moments was deciding to shelve an album, after working on it for a whole year, investing in it artistically, and putting out all that money.”
The project, aptly named Haganuz (“The Shelved”), sat locked away for nearly three years. By holding back the music until the market stabilized enough to listen, Nunu protected the integrity of the art, finally releasing it to critical acclaim earlier this month.
Owning the persona
When local artists mature, they often look for an exit strategy from their early, theatrical brands – much like Israeli rapper Ravid Plotnik dropping his moniker to perform under his real name.
But Aharoni-Gal isn’t interested in killing off her creation. Rejecting the idea that “Nunu” is a restrictive corporate mask, she views the colorful alter-ego as a direct, unfiltered extension of her real life.
“It’s not even a thought in my mind,” she clarifies firmly. “To me, Nunu is my name. In my art, I am 100% doing what I want and being exactly who I am. I write directly from my life experience, and it’s called Nunu, and that’s great and cool and no issue at all.”
The post-crisis road map
Now, her team is moving fast to make up for lost time. With ticket demand for her anniversary show instantly exhausting the Barby’s capacity, a second date has been added for December 2.
The strategy moving forward is a blitz of regional touring and diverse festival bookings. “We are going to take this show outside the walls of the Barby for a broader tour across Israel,” she reveals. “I’m also incredibly excited to hit the festival circuit soon – including performances at InDnegev, the Smilansky Festival, and likely the Eilat Piano Festival.”
Concurrently, she is entering a creative contraction phase to draft her next commercial statement. “Right now, creatively, I’m in that stage of turning inward, writing, and trying to understand what the next thing is that I want to say.”
Looking toward the decade mark
As she approaches her 28th birthday in two weeks, the superstition of the tragic “27 Club” is just an industry joke to be laughed off. “Yes, please! Let’s skip right past that club!” she laughs. Her focus is entirely on the long game.
When asked who she hopes will bring out her cake at her 10-year career milestone, she pointed to her close creative collaborator before aiming for the stars.
“You’ll have to ask Adam,” Nunu jokes, initially referring to her director, Adam Gabay. “He always surprises me. But honestly, for the 10-year mark, it really would be amazing if Adam Levine finally brought me the cake.”

Belarusian state TV says it planted ‘freelancers’ inside Current Time and handed over the names of more than 70 journalists to their home countries, mostly Russia — names that were already public
Employees of the Belarusian state television channel First Informational said they spent several years working with Alina Rudnitskaya, an editor at Current Time — the Russian-language TV and digital network run by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty in cooperation with Voice of America — while posing as freelancers.
The channel aired the segment on the evening of August 27, and the Telegram channel News.by later published excerpts from it.
The segment focuses largely on Rudnitskaya, claiming she flew from Russia to European Union countries 60 times over eight years.
According to the segment, those involved in the scheme obtained “the names of all employees who work for various Current Time bureaus around the world.” The list included more than 70 people, many of whom had already been named on Current Time’s website.
First Informational said it handed over the employees’ names “to the countries whose citizenship they hold,” meaning mainly Russian citizens.
